en: *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, Volume One, originally without omission; Chapter One: Enumeration of Titles.
Composed by Bodhisattva Sthiramati;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dao Tai and others of the Northern Liang dynasty.
1. Chapter on the Meaning (Arthavarga). Now, I wish to explain and enter into the meaning of the Mahāyāna. Question:
For what reason is the "Entry into the Meaning of the Mahāyāna" taught?
The answer is:
It is because I wish to prevent sentient beings from encountering the causes of suffering that you should now understand this.

Furthermore, there may be those who associate with evil friends and are led astray by evil; they cling one-sidedly to their own doctrines, are fixated on false views, and engage in inverted thinking. Failing to comprehend the true meaning and failing to accord with the Buddha’s wisdom, they slander the holy teachings. Those who slander the holy teachings thus destroy the True Dharma.
Those who destroy the True Dharma receive a retribution of great sin; as the World-Honored One has said:
"The sin of slandering the Dharma is heavier than the five heinous crimes; one will suffer the retribution of pain for a long duration in the evil realms."
As a verse says:
"Those who slander the Mahāyāna Dharma will certainly proceed to the evil realms;
that such a person receives this karmic retribution is what the One of True Wisdom has declared."
Born and fallen into hell, the great fires blaze upon one's body;
the burning is most agonizing—such indeed is the retribution for one's karmic offenses.
Great iron plows, blazing intensely, numbering fully five hundred, [plow across the ground].
His tongue is ploughed, and his entire body is shattered in agony.
If he escapes from hell, he undergoes further evil retributions:
his faculties are perpetually impaired and deficient, and he never hears the sound of the Dharma.
"Even if they should happen to hear it, they will again give rise to slander of the Dharma;
by the causal conditions of slandering the Dharma, they will fall back into hell.
When sentient beings who slander the Dharma hear such an exposition, they immediately conceive doubts regarding the Mahāyāna, as the Venerable Deva stated in verse:
"Those of meager merit do not give rise to doubt; those who can give rise to doubt will surely shatter all realms of existence (*bhava*).

All who have doubts should listen to the Dharma; having heard it, their minds will understand and they will attain awakening. Having attained awakening, they will immediately give rise to faith. Having given rise to faith, they will experience joy and bliss. Having experienced joy and bliss, they will thus successively give rise to hearing, reflection, and cultivation, until they fully realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)."

One falls into the evil realms because of slandering the Mahāyāna, yet it is also by means of the Mahāyāna that various wholesome karmas arise; it is like a person who falls to the ground and must rely upon that very ground to stand up again.

Furthermore, because one approaches the path to enlightenment by means of wisdom, one also exists in union with sentient beings; if one were separated from sentient beings, there would be no one who could attain the path to enlightenment.
The Bodhi of all Buddhas arises from the realm of sentient beings, as the Venerable Nāgārjuna stated in verse:
"It does not arise from space, Nor is it born from the element of earth;
It is realized and perfected within afflictions."
Question: You have spoken of the *Mahāyāna-praveśa-śāstra*.
By what characteristics is such merit called the Mahāyāna?
Answer: The section on the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is called Mahāyāna. Question:
"Does the Buddha not also teach the Mahāyāna, rather than the three vehicles?
He replied: "It is so."
In this Mahāyāna, it is also taught that the three vehicles are themselves called the Tripitaka.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, the Buddha addressed King Ajātaśatru: "Noble son!"
There are three types of Piṭaka. What are the three?
They are the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka, and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
O son of good family!

It is not because of the Śrāvaka vehicle that it is called the Tripiṭaka, nor is it because of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle that it is called the Tripiṭaka; only that which is studied by the Bodhisattvas—the Mahāyāna—is given the name Tripiṭaka.
Why is this? One who expounds the Dharma is called a Tripitaka-master only when they are fully endowed with the Three Vehicles.
Because the Bodhisattva’s exposition of the Dharma is able to encompass the Three Vehicles, it is for this reason that I designate it as the Tripitaka.
Noble son! There are three kinds of practitioners:
the śrāvaka training, the pratyekabuddha training, and the bodhisattva training.
Those of the Śrāvaka vehicle do not study the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
Why is this? Because it is not what they are capable of understanding.
Those of the Pratyekabuddhayāna do not study the Bodhisattvayāna. Why is this?
Because it is not what they understand.
Noble son! Although bodhisattvas study the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they do not realize the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Those who study the Bodhisattva Vehicle deeply understand the dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas and always delight in following them.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva Vehicle is called the Tripiṭaka, whereas the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not.
This has been explained in detail in other sūtras; therefore, I have now spoken only briefly. As for your view that there are not three piṭakas:

you should consider the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the *Madhyama Āgama*, the *Dīrgha Āgama*, and the *Saṃyukta Āgama*—consisting of hundreds of thousands of verses—as one piṭaka; and the Vinaya and Abhidharma, consisting of two hundred thousand verses, as the second piṭaka. When these are fully cultivated and mastered, they are called the three piṭakas.
If it were explained in this way, it would not be called the Tripiṭaka. Why is that?
Because other sūtras and so forth would then not be the Buddha's teaching; such would be the fault.
The Āgamas, Vinaya, Abhidharma, and so forth are also the Tripiṭaka.

The Kṣudrakapiṭaka, the Śatruñjaya-sūtra, the Garbha-sūtra, the *Rājavavādaka-jātaka*, the *Pratyekabuddha-nidāna*, and other such eighty-four thousand dharma-piṭakas that the Venerable Ānanda received and upheld from the Buddha—all of these likewise lack the fault of not being the Buddha’s word.
If there were no errors, one should know that all of it is the Buddha’s teaching.
If everything spoken in this manner were indeed the *piṭaka*, then there would be hundreds of thousands of such *piṭakas*.
Your statement regarding the Tripiṭaka contradicts itself.
Furthermore, there were things that Ānanda did not accept; it was only twenty years after the Buddha attained enlightenment that he spoke before the Saṃgha, saying:
"I am old and advanced in years, and I require someone to attend to my needs."
"If you can serve as my attendant, you should say yourself that you are able.
At that time, the great assembly reached a consensus and appointed Ānanda as the Buddha's attendant.
Ānanda then said to his fellow practitioners of the holy life:
"The Tathāgata possesses eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma, all of which I am now able to receive and uphold.
However, regarding those two bhikṣus who received and upheld [the teachings] during the first twenty years, I have not yet fully understood them."
For this reason, you should know that what Ānanda has received and upheld cannot be called "much learning.
Among the teachings spoken by the Buddha, there were indeed things for which Ānanda was not a fit vessel, as stated in the *Madhyama Āgama*, where Śakra Devānām Indra said to Uttara:
"Venerable One!"
Having attained the knowledge of others' minds, I observe all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa; there are none who are able to fully receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
With the sole exception of the Venerable One, no others can comprehend it.
For these reasons, you should know that Ānanda is not able to uphold all the Buddha-dharma.
That the śrāvaka disciples, including Ānanda, are not fit vessels for the Dharma has already been explained in detail throughout the Mahāyāna sūtras.
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, when the Buddha spoke to the Devaputra Viśuddhacandragarbha:
"That which Ānanda upholds is but a small amount, hardly worth mentioning; those who do not uphold it are, in fact, immeasurable."
Of the dharmas known to me, not even one part in a hundred thousand billion has been spoken; Ānanda, of the dharmas I have taught, he does not retain even one part in a hundred thousand billion.

"Good son! In a single day and night, the Brahmās, Śakras, Four Heavenly Kings, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and all the bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions gather before me. For them, I preach the sūtras, verses, and chapters on wisdom; I speak of the various pāramitās practiced by sentient beings; and I teach the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—disgust for birth and death, praise for nirvāṇa, and the fulfillment of the pāramitās. Even if I were to extensively expound the Dharma for all these sons of heaven for a full day and night, suppose there were as many learned and wise people filling Jambudvīpa as there are atoms of dust, all equal to Ānanda: even in a hundred thousand billion parts of what they could retain in a single day and night, they would not be able to hold even one part."
Even if one were to fill as many worlds in the ten directions as there are atoms with individuals like Ānanda, they likewise would be unable to fully uphold [the teachings].
This is also stated in various sūtras: that Ānanda was not fit to be a vessel for the Dharma.
For this reason, it should be understood that Ānanda cannot fully uphold all the Buddha’s teachings.
A question is asked:
Did not the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, say that Ānanda is the foremost among those of great learning?
The answer is:
The Buddha provisionally designated Ānanda as the foremost among the assembly of śrāvakas, but this does not refer to bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, you yourselves have not even heard all that was held by Ānanda, let alone the Mahāyāna which possesses its complete and profound meaning!
If you think that the Śrāvaka vehicle is itself the Mahāyāna, this is not so.
Why? Because cause and effect are distinct.
If the causes of the Śrāvaka vehicle were not different from the causes of the Mahāyāna, their results would likewise not be different.
Since we observe that the results are indeed different, one should know that the causes are also different.
Why is this? Those who study as śrāvakas merely sever the obstacles of the fetters, contemplate the practice of impermanence, and hear the Dharma from others.

The bodhisattvas, however, sever even the subtle habitual tendencies; they contemplate all phenomena until reaching the ultimate emptiness, attaining spontaneous wisdom and teacherless wisdom without relying on hearing it from others.
For this reason, the Śrāvaka vehicle is not identical to the Mahāyāna.
Question: The Buddha did not say that there is no difference between [their] liberations.
The answer is:

When a śrāvaka attains liberation, can he cause Mount Sumeru and all such things to turn toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and bow down completely; can his radiance illuminate the worlds of the ten directions, and can he cause all the hosts of Māra within eighty yojanas to come and submit?
The liberation of a bodhisattva can accomplish all that has been described above.

For this reason, although the Buddha taught in other sūtras that the characteristics of liberation are identical and without difference, there is in fact a distinction between the Great and the Small Vehicles.
It is like a mustard seed hollowed out by insects; although it bears the name "empty," could this emptiness be made one with the emptiness of the worlds in the ten directions?
Although emptiness is not different, there is a distinction between their sizes.
Furthermore, it is like wishing for a firefly to equal the sun and moon, or like comparing a mosquito to a garuḍa.
As the bhikṣu Śāriputra said in the verses on the Buddha’s past conduct:
"Of all lights in existence, Whether the flame of a lamp or a flash of lightning,"
The stars and moon differ in their illumination, yet the sunlight is foremost among them.
Among the various winged creatures and beasts— the mosquitoes, ants, and bees,
and the many birds that fly in diverse ways— the garuḍa is most distinct.
For this reason, although there is some slight resemblance, there is a distinction between the Great and the Small.
You should know that since the causes are already different, how could the fruits be the same?
As for your claim that liberation is without difference, when examined in this way, liberations are not the same.

The liberation of the śrāvakas is called "liberation through the exhaustion of craving," yet it is not universal liberation; it is merely a provisional distinction taught for the sake of sentient beings with dull faculties and little wisdom.

The liberation of the Mahāyāna, however, involves the severance of the habitual tendencies of afflictions such that they are entirely exhausted; this is extensively and analytically explained for the sake of bodhisattvas with sharp faculties.
If, as you now say, the liberation of the śrāvakas is identical to the liberation of the Mahāyāna, then the Tathāgata would not possess omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);
such would be the fault.
For example, when the Buddha was slightly ill, he sent Maudgalyāyana to the place of Jīvaka to inquire what medicine should be prescribed.
At that time, it had already been seven days since Kṣemaka had passed away, and he had been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Maudgalyāyana immediately went to that celestial realm. Then, as Kṣemaka was about to enter the rear garden, he asked:
"The Tathāgata is ill; what medicine does he require?"
He replied:
"Ghee is used.
The body of the Tathāgata is like a diamond; since all evils have been extinguished, how could there be illness? Why then do you ask about Jīvaka?"
For example, the bhikṣu Bakula, because he gave a single medicinal fruit to a fellow practitioner of the holy life ninety kalpas ago, remained free from illness throughout those ninety kalpas.
In his final existence, even at the age of eighty, he was never afflicted by the slightest ailment.

If by the mere cause of this slight gift of a single *harītakī* fruit he attained freedom from illness, how much more so for the Tathāgata, who throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas fulfilled the *dānapāramitā* and perfected all merits—even to the point of cutting off his own hands, feet, marrow, brain, blood, and flesh to give them to the sick—how could he possibly fall ill because of such causes and conditions?
If it were as stated in the sūtras, it would imply that the Tathāgata is not omniscient.
Furthermore, there are times when the Tathāgata enters a city to beg for alms and returns with an empty bowl.

For the sake of delivering Devadatta and causing him to leave the household life—as described in the *Śuṣkavṛkṣa-sūtra*—he saw a great mass of fire, at which time some among the bhikṣus conceived thoughts of regressing from their resolve.
In order to deliver the horse trainer, Pūrṇamāsa, and others, he repeatedly reviled the Brahmins,
the Rājagṛhas, the Sāṃkhyas, the Nirgranthas,
Sundarī, and so forth.
During the ninety days [of the famine], he consumed horse barley; Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra entered a pottery kiln—such were the events that occurred.
If you think that there remained further karma [to be exhausted], [then consider this].
This is not so. Why? Because the Tathāgata has exhausted all evils and is fully endowed with all immeasurable merits.

If there were remaining evil karma, there would be great transgression; have you not heard it stated in the various sūtras that the Tathāgata has forever severed all afflictions, karmic actions, fetters, and habitual tendencies?
As in the verse of praise spoken by Mātṛceṭa:
"All fetters and habitual tendencies are exhausted; there remains only the Savior of the World.
Whatever belongs to the Omniscient One, all his merits are fully perfected."

There are three kinds of habitual tendencies: namely, the habituation of karma, the habituation of afflictions, and the habituation of deportment. These three kinds of habitual tendencies have been eternally exhausted by the Tathāgata.
For this reason, if there were any remaining karma, it would be a great fault.
If you now claim that this is a skillful means (upāya), this is also not the case.
Why? Because your previous intention was to maintain that the Buddha-body is real, and you did not say it was a skillful means or an emanation (nirmāṇa).
"You have often said yourself that the Buddha-body is one; how then can there be expedient means and responsive transformations?
In which sutra have you heard it taught that there are expedient means and responsive transformations?"

In your sūtra, you state that there is only the "final body" (paścima-deha), and you do not say that there is a distinct dharma-body (dharma-kāya) different from the transformation-body (nirmāṇa-kāya) and the expedient body (upāya-kāya).
However, what I have taught in my *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* is that there is a distinct dharma-body, which is not the same as the expedient or transformation bodies.
Therefore, when the Mahāyāna sūtras state that the Buddha is omniscient, there is no fault;
however, when you of the Hīnayāna claim [the Buddha] is omniscient, there is a great error.
If it is claimed that the Śrāvakayāna is itself the Mahāyāna, this is not so.
There is a distinction between the Mahāyāna and the Śrāvakayāna, because the former is vast and extensive.
If you think that the Mahāyāna is revealed within the Śrāvaka vehicle, this is also not the case. Why?
Because it contradicts reason.
Those of the Śrāvaka vehicle hear the Dharma from others; the vehicle of the Great Sage ensures that the lineage of the Three Jewels continues without interruption.
It is like a lapis lazuli gem, which can never emerge from within crystal, because their essential natures are distinct.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna is subtle, profound, and its mind is vast.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in successive stages, from the first ground through to the tenth, fully perfecting all meritorious qualities, wisdom, and karmic activities; for this reason, the Buddha calls it the Mahāyāna Vehicle.
If the Śrāvaka vehicle were to emerge from the Mahāyāna, that would indeed be logical.
Therefore, because Bodhisattvas cultivate and study the ten stages (daśabhūmi) and fully perfect all the pāramitās, they are able to give rise to the wholesome dharmas of the three vehicles.
As stated in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the system of phonemes (*akṣara-mātṛkā*); the root phonemes are the beginning, for all written characters emerge from these root phonemes."
In this way, O Son of the Buddha!
All Buddha-dharmas are likewise: taking the stages (bhūmi) as the beginning, they also proceed from these stages to achieve the ultimate perfection of spontaneous wisdom (svayambhū-jñāna).
Therefore, the Mahāyāna is called "profound," for it gives birth to all the merits of the śrāvakas; it does not mean that the Hīnayāna can produce the Great Vehicle.
The Buddha taught the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi), which are like a mass of gold complete and without flaw; why would one not accept them?
The Tathāgata, by the power of his compassion, taught the Śrāvaka-yāna for the sake of those with dull faculties.
Yet you, having accepted it, have become biased and attached, practicing only the minor teachings while failing to believe in the Mahāyāna’s impartial and correct doctrine.
Therefore, one should know that the Buddha has declared the Mahāyāna to be the most auspicious and supreme.
Question: The World-Honored One previously said:
In the future world after my parinirvāṇa, there will be many sentient beings who give rise to various disputes, saying, "This was spoken by the Buddha; this was not spoken by the Buddha.

Therefore, the Tathāgata seals them with the Dharma-seal: if the meaning enters into the Sūtras, accords with the Vinaya, and does not contradict the characteristics of the Dharma, it is called the word of the Buddha.
The answer is:
The Buddha also did not say that the Śrāvaka vehicle is not my teaching; even so it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna.
The Buddha’s teachings are not different, for they are all of one single characteristic, sealed by the Dharma-seal.
Regarding what you say about "entering," does this mean entering the sūtras in their meaning, or entering them through their words?
If it were by means of entering through words, that would be impossible.
Why is this? Because the texts, verses, and phrases of the twelve divisions of the scriptures each differ; therefore, one should know that entry is not by means of words.
If one enters by means of meaning, there is no contradiction in principle.

Regarding "meaning" (*artha*): if it accords with the meaning of the sūtras and its significance manifests in correspondence with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it is therefore called "accordant with the sūtras."
If it reveals the Dharma of the śrāvakas, it is called the Śrāvaka-yāna, which accords with and enters into the Sūtras.
If it reveals the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas, it is called the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, which accords with and enters into the Sūtras.
If one reveals the dharmas of a bodhisattva, it is called the Bodhisattvayāna; this accords with and enters into the sūtras.
If I reveal the merits of the ten stages and clarify the conduct of a bodhisattva, this is called the true teaching; it accords with and enters into the Mahāyāna.
However, your mind is biased and partisan, for you claim that [the threefold training] enters only the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna.
I have already explained that it enters the Tripiṭaka of the Mahāyāna; therefore, the Tripiṭaka itself is the Mahāyāna.
Why is this? Among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is said that the Vaipulya is precisely the Mahāyāna.
As stated in the *Madhyama Āgama*, what is meant by "kūṭakūṭa"?
What is called "knowledge of the Dharma" refers to being able to skillfully understand the twelve divisions of the scriptures, from the Sūtras up to the Upadeśas.
Among these, the Vaipulya is the Mahāyāna.

Why is this? The Vaipulya sūtras are called *vaipulya* because they teach the methods for cultivating remedies for all sentient beings; they are called *vaipulya* because they contain many diverse vehicles (*yāna*); they are called *vaipulya* because they possess many ornaments; they are called *vaipulya* because they can produce immeasurable great fruits of retribution; they are called *vaipulya* because they cannot be known through mere calculation or measurement; and they are called *vaipulya* because they eliminate and sever all false views.
If you think that within my teaching for the śrāvakas, the extensive sūtras, verses, and prose passages are also called Vaipulya, that is not the case.
Why is this? You rely on the Āgamas and claim they are Vaipulya, yet these are merely words.
If they are merely words, they are not to be trusted.
If this meaning were necessarily present within the *Āgama* sūtras, in which specific passage would it be stated that the *Vaipulya* was taught for the sake of the śrāvakas?
Since there is no such definitive text, one should know that the *Vaipulya* elucidates the Mahāyāna; it does not refer to the teachings of the śrāvaka Hīnayāna.
In the single collection of Sūtras for the Śrāvakas that you preach, there are ultimately not even a hundred thousand verses of praise and prose, let alone tens of billions of extensive expositions.

When the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, instructs the Śrāvakas, he reveals only impermanence to cause them to weary of birth and death, and enables them to know the root of suffering so they may swiftly seek Nirvāṇa.
From the beginning "thus" up to "practicing accordingly," if the words and meanings were meager, there would be no profound or vast significance.
The Mahāyāna sūtras describe the deeds of bodhisattvas, and those matters are profound and extensive.
As in the *Mahā-upama-sūtra*, the *Bhadrakalpika-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Vimukti-sūtra*, and the *Puṣpamūla-sūtra*—all such works as these belong to the Mahāyāna and are all termed Vaipulya.

As it is said in the *Sūtra on the Binding and Liberation*: the youth Sudhana went to the presence of the spiritual friend, the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, and for twelve years entered the samādhi of the Great Ocean. He then addressed Sāgaramegha, saying:
"This samādhi is profound, vast, and boundless; is there any further dharma-gate greater than this samādhi?"

Having spoken these words, within the Samādhi of the Great Ocean he saw a great lotus flower, from which a Buddha emerged; he then stroked the crown of Sāgaradhvaja’s head with his right hand and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Noble son! There is yet another Dharma-door called the Universal Eye; you should receive and uphold it.
Sāgaradhvaja then received the verses and phrases of the Universal Eye Dharma-door and explained them extensively for others in successive order, saying to Sudhana:

"Good son! Regarding the Universal Eye Dharma-gate that I have upheld in a single kṣaṇa, even if one were to use all the waters of the great ocean to grind into ink, pile up great sheets of paper as high as Mount Sumeru, take all the grasses and trees under heaven to serve as pens, and employ every sentient being on land and in water throughout the trichiliocosm as scribes, they could not transcribe even one-hundred-thousandth part of the Dharma-gate received in that single kṣaṇa. How much less could they record the profound, immeasurable, and boundless essential meanings received over the course of one day and night, or even twelve years?"

Having heard the Dharma from a single spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the youth Sudhana was able to attain such immeasurable and boundless [realizations] exceeding thousands of millions; how much more so when he had consulted with the Buddhas throughout worlds as numerous as atoms, as well as received the teachings from his spiritual friends?
For these reasons, the Mahāyāna is fully endowed with the name *Vibhaṅga* (analytical exposition); it is immeasurable and boundless, unlike that of the śrāvakas.

This meaning is profoundly deep; therefore, all dharmas practiced by the śrāvakas entirely enter the path of the Mahāyāna, which is the most auspicious. This is called "conforming to the meaning of the Sūtras."
Now I shall further explain the Vinaya that accords with the truth.
The noble paths of the three vehicles are all identical in their severing of greed, hatred, and delusion; this is called Vinaya.
The Sūtras distinguish between cause and effect.
The Abhidharma distinguishes the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and also severs the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Mahāyāna likewise teaches the severance of all evil dharmas, including the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.
In Buddhism, the purification of one's own three karmas by the śrāvakas is called Vinaya;

for bodhisattvas, it is taught as the purification of one's own three karmas until the attainment of Buddhahood, while simultaneously bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment through the perfection of all śīla-pāramitās.
The precepts maintained by a bodhisattva are those of their own nature; by generating the mind of enlightenment, they attain the fruit of reality.
Therefore, one should know that the Mahāyāna accords with the vinaya.

"Not contradicting the characteristics of the Dharma" means that the sūtras of the Three Vehicles do not contradict the twelve links of dependent origination, and the Mahāyāna likewise does not contradict the twelve links of dependent origination.
One who observes skillfully can know that the Mahāyāna is itself the Three Seals of the Dharma; if one does not observe skillfully, then there is no Mahāyāna, nor are the Three Vehicles complete.

To slander the Mahāyāna is a grave transgression. If you now say that this is the teaching of Māra and was not spoken by the Buddha, yet such words do not actually exist within the various sūtras—if one merely speaks of it as the Mahāyāna with one's mouth alone, this is the teaching of Māra and is ultimately not to be trusted.
If you think that this was spoken by the Buddha, it would be like insects born from within a lion's body devouring the lion itself.
This applies to all three vehicles, not just the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, that which accords with the Mahāyāna is beyond the reach of Māra; only a Buddha can speak it.
[The opponent] asks:
"Is it not you who are speaking the words of Māra, while I am the one who speaks the truth?"
He replied, "I and you are both not Māras. He asked:
If you claim that neither I nor you are Māras, yet say that what we speak is the teaching of Māra, then this must be refuted.
The answer is:

Because my Mahāyāna Dharma benefits sentient beings and accords with the characteristics of reality (dharmalakṣaṇa), demonic obstacles abound; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of "refuting Māra" within the Mahāyāna.
Your Hīnayāna dharma can only deliver oneself; since demons do not disturb or afflict you, why would there be a need to obstruct [others]?

For this reason, the Tathāgata previously taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras* that in future ages, many sentient beings will take pleasure in giving rise to jealousy; therefore, they will obstruct and slander [the Mahāyāna], falling into the evil realms.
In which of the scriptural divisions (*nikāya*) that you recite and study does it state that the Mahāyāna was spoken by Māra?
If your own scriptures do not state that the Mahāyāna was spoken by Māra, then your claim that it was spoken by Māra is likewise untrustworthy.
If you think that there is also a negation [of the self] within the Śrāvaka teachings, but that it has long since ceased to exist and is therefore difficult to verify— this is not so. Why is that?
Because it is not a place where [the Dharma] could perish.
Even if one were to attempt to obstruct it, the Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, would be able to protect this Dharma so that it does not fall into oblivion even throughout kalpas.
Therefore, you should know that your claim regarding its long duration is merely words.

Even if it were spoken by Māra, if it can eliminate the obstacles of delusion and does not contradict the True Dharma, then although it is called "Māra’s teaching," it is in fact the True Dharma and is no different from the Buddha’s words.
Why is this? As the Buddha has taught, one should rely on the Dharma and not rely on the person; therefore, I now follow only correct principle and do not grasp at mere names.

Furthermore, the one we seek who can extinguish the cognitive obscurations and the afflictive obscurations is the World-Honored One himself; if he were truly a Māra, he could never have preached the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Māra cannot know that the bodhisattva gives rise to the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation from meditative concentration.
That the wearying detachment from desires and unwholesome states is the meaning of the Mahāyāna can only be taught by a Buddha.

From the first stage through to the tenth stage, in this sequential order, there are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, the bodhicitta, and the various pāramitās—these being the methods for maturing and gathering sentient beings through appropriate skillful means.
The ten paths of wholesome action, ethical discipline, learning, wisdom, heedfulness, detachment from the eight worldly dharmas,
the noble eightfold path, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the merit of maintaining the dhūta ascetic practices,
suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and cessation, the twelve links of dependent origination, the entering and emerging from the various dhyānas, and the three gates of liberation.
All dhāraṇīs, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the various gates of supernormal powers,
the true truths and the four analytical knowledges, and the two wheels of dhyāna and wisdom—
all these adornments are perfectly integrated; they sport within all phenomena, neither turning their back on saṃsāra nor heading toward nirvāṇa.
With a mind of constant revulsion, they correctly contemplate the various stages and transcend them, not falling into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; they purify Buddha-fields,
accord with the patience regarding dharmas and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas,
and attain the stage of non-retrogression and the stage of entering the fixed position, as well as the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, and the marks and signs.
The Dharma-body, for the sake of sentient beings, dwells within birth and death; it follows the turning and the determinate turning, and it accords with non-turning and the determinate non-turning.
Such sequential dharmas of cause and effect, the unshared dharmas, and the dharmas not realized by others cannot be spoken of by Māra, because they are not within the realm of Māra.
There are four kinds of Māras. If one were to say that this was spoken by the Skandha-māra, I would never say that the Buddha possesses a body of aggregates (skandha-kāya).
Furthermore, if it were truly spoken by Māra, then even Maitreya Bodhisattva should have refuted such words.

Furthermore, the Venerable Piṇḍola, the Venerable Rāhula, and other such sixteen great śrāvakas were scattered across various islands; as also stated in other sūtras, there were ninety-nine billion great arhats who all took voting sticks before the Buddha to protect the Dharma and remain in this world for the duration of its lifespan.

In the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, on the islands of wheat, millet, and lions, on Jambudvīpa and Mahājambudvīpa, at the site of Badarīka, in Kaśmīra, and as far as Lake Anavatapta—there dwell all the worthy sages and holy ones, who protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
If one were to say that the Mahāyāna was spoken by Māra, it would constitute a great affliction for the Buddha-dharma, and all the worthy sages and saints should have obstructed and severed it.
Therefore, you should know that those who claim it was spoken by Māra are merely uttering falsehoods; they speak thus in vain.
Furthermore, the great bodhisattvas and all the noble ones protect the Mahāyāna; this Mahāyāna ensures that the lineage of the Three Jewels continues and is not allowed to be severed.
Question: According to what you have said, if the Mahāyāna is the seed of the Three Jewels, then it protects all bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Now, why do you not restrain those who slander the Mahāyāna, so that such people may not fall into hell, not proceed toward the evil realms, and not destroy the Buddha-dharma?
The answer is:
Karmic retribution is determinate and cannot be eliminated or severed.

There are two kinds of karma: first, that which is determinately increasing; second, that which is determinately to be experienced as retribution. These cannot be extinguished by any bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, or noble ones (ārya).
When one has committed evil karma, the retribution is certain and cannot be averted.
For example, the bhikṣu Kokālika slandered the Mahāyāna sūtras, claiming they were spoken by Māra; it should be known that such a person will inevitably fall into hell, and no one can rescue him.
Question: Your statement that one who slanders the Mahāyāna will enter the evil realms is also a harsh word; I do not yet believe it.
The answer is:

Your claim that the Buddha’s teaching of the Mahāyāna is the word of Māra is itself a slander against the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and it constitutes a great enmity toward all sentient beings.
What has been spoken was extremely coarse and fierce; one shall receive the heavy retribution for unwholesome harsh speech, as the Buddha’s verse says:
“Human beings born into this world Are like an axe held within their mouths;
They cut and harm their own bodies— All of this arises from evil karma.”
"You have slandered the Mahāyāna; such coarse speech was not spoken by me.
I now speak these words for your benefit, solely desiring that you do not give rise to further slanders."

It is just as when a patient eats what should not be eaten; a skilled physician, observing the illness, forbids and prohibits it out of compassion for you, lest you falsely engage in frivolous speech by claiming that the Mahāyāna was spoken by Māra.

The Buddhas of the past have already taught the Mahāyāna; the Buddhas of the future shall teach the Mahāyāna; and the Buddhas of the present are now teaching the Mahāyāna. This is called the discourse that prevents and cuts off the slander of the Mahāyāna.
In order to sever slander against the Mahāyāna, the Bodhisattva therefore expounds the "Chapter on the Initial Entry into the Mahāyāna-śāstra.
A question is asked:
"You have already refuted others so as not to allow them to slander; how, then, should one now enter into the practice of the Mahāyāna?"
The answer is:
A bodhisattva should first be endowed with the spiritual lineage (gotra), conforming to wholesome conduct, possessing vast understanding, a vast inner mind, vast elements (dhātu), and a vast lineage.

Since their nature is already complete, their minds are harmonious and supple; they gradually diminish their afflictions, reducing greed, hatred, and delusion, while delighting in the cultivation of various virtues and applying themselves with diligence to recitation and study.
Thus, these sentient beings possess vast six sense-faculties and are able to give rise to great vows, desiring to seek the Buddha-way.
Their dispositions and characteristics are as the Buddha has described:
those with inferior faculties, inferior natures, and who have generated the aspiration for the Way in an inferior manner, their vows are likewise inferior.
Those of middling faculties, middling natures, and middling arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment have middling aspirations;
those of superior faculties, superior natures, and superior arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment have superior aspirations.
Therefore, the Buddhas, according to their faculties and natures, provide instruction through compassionate discernment. Question:
If all sentient beings each possess their own faculties and natures, how should one preach the Dharma in accordance with those faculties?

Answer: For sentient beings of superior faculties, he expounds the profound and wondrous Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas; because he knows their root-natures are capable of the Bodhisattva practice, he teaches the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Question: In what stage should one who maintains the Bodhisattva-piṭaka abide? Answer:
There are ten kinds of practices for reaching the stage of liberation.
When one is able to hear the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one attains ten kinds of dharma-practices; by departing from [limited] practices for liberation, one then enters into the practice of a bodhisattva.
What are the ten? First, one cultivates the liberative practices of a bodhisattva, practicing them all, whether they be many or few.
Second, one transcribes all the teachings possessed by a bodhisattva, whether they be many or few.
Third, one should make offerings to all teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, whether they be many or few.
Fourth, one should recite and read all the teachings of the Bodhisattvas, whether they be many or few.
Fifth, regarding the Dharma of a bodhisattva, whether it be much or little, one listens to and receives it all.
Sixth, regarding the Dharma of a bodhisattva, whether it be much or little, one upholds and maintains it all.
Seventh, it is the dharma of a bodhisattva that whether much or little, they shall all practice recitation until they gradually master them.
Eighth, it is the dharma of a bodhisattva that whether much or little, they shall all analyze and expound them for others.
Ninth, it is the dharma of a bodhisattva that whether much or little, they reflect upon and thoroughly understand the meaning and intent of all things.
Tenth, it is the dharma of a bodhisattva that whether much or little, they dwell alone in reflection to cultivate, accumulate, and further clarify their understanding.
These are called the ten practices of a bodhisattva.
The eighth is the bodhisattva’s wisdom derived from hearing; the ninth is the bodhisattva’s wisdom derived from reflection; and the tenth is the bodhisattva’s wisdom derived from cultivation.
Question: Once a bodhisattva has attained this hearing, reflection, and cultivation, into what practice should they enter? Answer:
In order to attain one's own stage and enter the gates of liberation, one generates [wisdom] through hearing, reflection, and cultivation in this sequential manner;
to perceive the dharma-realm and attain one's own stage, one cultivates the three gates of liberation.
Question: What are called the three gates of liberation? Answer:
One practices emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Question: What is meant by emptiness?
Answer: One contemplates that the self, persons, and sentient beings have no intrinsic substance, and that their nature and characteristics are eternally quiescent. Question:
How is it understood?
The answer is:
one should enter into the twelve links of dependent origination.
Question: Is this liberation through emptiness different from the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination? Answer:

Emptiness and the twelve links of dependent origination are identical and without difference; emptiness is itself the twelve links of dependent origination, and the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves emptiness. Why is this so?
Arising through causes and conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature.
As the Venerable Nāgārjuna said in verse:
"The twelve links of dependent origination are empty; I now wish to explain them."
"Conditioned phenomena are merely provisional names; this itself is the Middle Way.
All dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent. Why is this so?
All things belong to causes and conditions, for they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Question:
If all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, why do you say that they have no substantial essence?
Answer: What is called "causes and conditions" is spoken of from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is neither intrinsic nature nor arising; since there is no arising, there is also no cessation. That which is without arising and without cessation is true quiescence (*śānti*); true quiescence is the quiescence of all phenomena (*dharma*). Therefore, I say that all phenomena have no intrinsic nature.
As the Blessed One said in the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*:
"Sister!
For example, it is by depending on a person, a drumstick, and a drum—through the conjunction of these various conditions—that sound arises."
Such sounds do not exist within the three periods of time, nor are they internal, external, or in between.
Their nature is empty and quiescent, without arising and without ceasing.
Sister, you should now know that the essential nature of all phenomena is likewise so.

In the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, the Buddha himself spoke of emptiness; therefore, throughout immeasurable kalpas, Bodhisattvas cultivate and accumulate merit, meditative concentration, and wisdom, all of which enter the gateways of the three liberations.
One should skillfully contemplate that arising and ceasing are entirely empty and quiescent, like an illusion, a mirage, or a city of the Gandharvas—all identical to dream-visions.
As the Buddha said:
"When one first awakens to the twelve links of dependent origination, one realizes that all sentient beings are entirely empty."
"What is attained in a single kṣaṇa is like a magical illusion, a mirage, or a city of the Gandharvas.
Thus, entering the gate of liberation of emptiness in successive stages, his mind was filled with joy, and he attained the ultimate benefit.
Question: The non-Buddhists each cling to the view of a self; how is this to be refuted and severed? Answer:
In this way, these non-Buddhists give rise to defiled attachment toward both internal and external forms; they grasp at a self and what belongs to a self, following the current of birth and death.
Those who are attached to a self think, "I am able to bestow food, drink, wealth, and profit."
In this way, there are various [notions] based on the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding "self" and "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*): that which is created by the self is the "self," while things such as jars and other objects are called "what belongs to the self. These are what one relies upon.

Regarding the karma they have performed—whether as identical, different, both identical and different, or neither identical nor different—they cling to these views with partiality and attachment, merely using words to deceive the world and themselves.
For this reason, they transmigrate through birth and death, failing to understand that all phenomena arising from causes and conditions are empty of intrinsic nature. Question:
These non-Buddhists fail to understand dependent origination and give rise to four types of clinging; what is the fault in this?
The answer is:
According to what the Sāṃkhya school teaches, there is the error of conceiving [things] as one.
To regard the action and the agent as one, the characteristic and the characterized as one, and the part and the whole as one—all such instances are termed "one."

The Ulūka school calculates difference; the Nirgrantha school calculates both unity and difference; the Ajita school calculates neither unity nor difference; and all other heterodox views, such as those of the Māthara school and others, do not deviate from these four types of calculation.
Question: The Sāṃkhya proponents say that the action and the agent are one and the same; what fault is there in this? Answer:
Because speech has two aspects, it is not called "one.
The act is the cause and the agent is the effect; since these things are distinct, how can they be said to be one?
To claim they are one when they are actually different is a perversion.
Why is this? Because the agent is identical to the action.
Since the action and the agent differ in terms of temporal sequence, how could they be one?
Question: The function is the same before and after, just as a seed produces a sprout.
Although there is a temporal sequence, because they are a similar continuity, it is called "one."
The answer is:
This too has a fault.
If the action exists prior and the agent exists posteriorly, then since the produced and the unproduced are distinct, how can they be one?
For example, just as a pot and its parts can never coexist simultaneously, and just as the horns of an ox do not arise dependent upon one another, so it is with the action and the agent.

Furthermore, the reason why the action and the agent cannot be identical is that their sounds are distinct, their meanings are distinct, their causes and conditions are distinct, their times are distinct, their characters are distinct, and their essences are distinct.
If it were so, there would be many fallacies.
If it were merely one, it should not have two names;
because the sound, meaning, substance, and characteristics differ in their sequence, they cannot be considered one.
If the action were identical to the agent, then just as when one takes a lump of clay, the potter, the wheel, the string, the curd, and the butter would all necessarily be obtained [as the agent].
Since they are not so obtained, one should know that they are not one.
Just as my mind cannot be established as a single entity—if it were a single entity, then because the mind is impermanent, the self would also have to be impermanent.

For this reason, the agent and the action, the characteristic and the characterized, the measure and the measured, and the part and the whole are all equally refuted; even the existence of a single jar and so forth should likewise be refuted and negated.

Just as [the identity of] form and the jar must be refuted, so too must the production of such things as white cotton cloth and blue leaves, or length, shortness, squareness, and roundness, be refuted.
Question: What fault is there in the Vaiśeṣika teacher’s doctrine of difference?
The answer is:
If the action were different from the agent, there would likewise be a great fault.
The question is:
"What is the fault?
We only pray that you will explain it. He replied:
If the jar were different from the clay, then when making a jar one should take thread, and when making cloth one should take clay.
Since one does not take thread when making a jar, it should be known that they are not different.
Furthermore, a lump of clay is formed from atoms, and a jar is formed from the lump of clay.
If the jar were different from the lump of clay, the jar would have no substantial reality.
Since the jar is produced from the lump of clay, they cannot be different.

The lump of clay is the agent with respect to the atoms, and it is the agent with respect to the jar. If the action were different from the agent, then the clay would differ from the atoms only in name relative to the jar; there should not be two [distinct entities].
For this reason, the action and the agent cannot be distinct.
The production of cotton cloth from threads and the making of a mat from *po* grass are both explained in the same way.
Furthermore, if there were a distinction between the pot and its existence, then all phenomena would be undermined.
Why is this? If there were a single entity that was not a jar, then a jar would have to exist apart from it.
If there were a single entity that was a jar, then there would be many jars.
Because "non-identity" would follow from "difference," then difference itself should also be non-existent;
thus, there would be no jar. For this reason, your conception of difference destroys all phenomena.
Question: One who speaks in this manner does not destroy all dharmas. Why is that?
There is that which exists by depending on the jar; therefore, the existence of "one" and so forth regarding the jar is established.
The answer is:
if "one" were conjoined with the jar, then "one" should be the jar itself.
If the pot were conjoined with "existence," then the pot itself should also be called "existent," for since it is conjoined with existence, it cannot be distinct from it.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that "existence" is different [from the pot], this is like the case of white cotton cloth; this too entails a logical error.
Why is this? Whiteness is not the cotton cloth, nor is the cotton cloth whiteness; whiteness and the cotton cloth are distinct, and the same applies to other things.
For example, when the cotton cloth is burned, the whiteness should not be burned; if the whiteness were also burned when the cotton cloth is burned, they could not be considered distinct.
Now, you claim that words and things differ and that their characteristics differ;
this is not so. Your previous assertion that the six categories are each distinct must be refuted. Question:
Nigaṇṭha, what fault is there in first asserting identity or difference?
He replied:
Regarding what you call identity or difference—whether one says that the action and the agent are identical, or says that the action and the agent are different—this too entails many faults.
Question: What fault is there? Answer:
If the action were identical to the agent, the action would not be established.
If the action were different from the agent, the action likewise would not be established. Why is this so?
Since cause and effect are distinct, how can they be one?
Because the fruit is produced through a multitude of conditions, they cannot be considered different.
This is likewise true for the characteristics of the action and the characteristics of the agent.

Question: Just as the characteristics of a jar are destroyed while its substance is not destroyed, it can also be considered "different" because the substance remains even though the characteristics are destroyed. This is because we observe that while the substance persists, the characteristics perish.
If, when a jar is broken, its original substantial entity ceases to exist, it cannot be considered different [from the shards].
The reply is:
if one asserts they are identical, one falls into the same error as the Sāṃkhya school.
If one says they are different, this is refuted by the same reasoning used against the Vaiśeṣika teacher.
This also refutes all cases such as "the leaf is green" or "the cotton cloth is white. Question:
If Pūraṇa Kāśyapa maintains that [the self and the body] are neither identical nor different, what fault is there?
The answer is:
each of the three preceding views has its own respective attachment.
If you say they are not one, they ought to be different;
if you say they are not different, they ought to be one.
For what reason do you maintain that they are neither one nor different?
If one has no attachment yet speaks falsely, then one destroys the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Question: You say that even in the Mahāyāna there is no attachment; you, too, should therefore destroy all characteristics of dharmas.
The answer is:
That which I maintain is that what is perceived in the world is the dharma of dependent origination.
What you have stated is merely a perversion, as it does not accord with the characteristics of dharmas.
Question: What is the characteristic of dharmas (dharma-lakṣaṇa), such that you say it destroys the characteristic of dharmas? Answer:
That which is without the characteristics of a substance is itself the characteristic of a substance. Question:
How is it that being without the characteristics of a substance constitutes the characteristic of a substance?
Answer: Emptiness means the absence of essential nature and characteristics. Question:
What is meant by "emptiness"?
Is it empty because of existence, or is it empty because of non-existence?
The answer is:

I do not call it "emptiness" because of the meaning of existence, nor do I call it "emptiness" because of the meaning of non-existence; it is called "emptiness" because it is free from both existence and non-existence.
As the Venerable Nāgārjuna said in verse:
"To cling to existence is called eternalism; To reckon in non-existence is nihilism."
"If one is free from both existence and non-existence, this is called true emptiness.
Furthermore, as stated in a verse in Nāgārjuna’s *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*:
"To cling to existence is to grasp at substantial characteristics; to cling to non-existence is to be attached to the absence of substance."
"Not abiding in existence or non-existence—this is called the true contemplation.
For this reason, being free from existence and non-existence is called emptiness; because it is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, it is called the Middle Way.
If one can awaken to such characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), one is therefore called a Buddha.
For this reason, the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination is termed "emptiness" (śūnyatā). Question:
By what evidence is it known that the twelve links of dependent origination are empty?
The answer is:
for example, consider a jar; it is formed only after the combination of various conditions, such as a lump of clay, a wheel, a string, and a potter.
The lump of clay is not itself the jar, nor does the jar exist apart from the lump of clay.
It is merely designated by the conventional name "jar," dependent upon a multitude of causes and conditions, and possesses no intrinsic essence or characteristic.
Because there is no essential nature (*svabhāva*), there is no arising; because there is no arising, essential nature is quiescent.
That which is produced by causes and conditions lacks an essential nature.

If all phenomena were to possess a determinate self-nature independent of causes and conditions, such a thing would be impossible, for since they lack their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the jar does not exist; and since the jar does not exist, all phenomena likewise do not exist.
As the Venerable Deva said in verse:
"If even a single phenomenon has an intrinsic nature, then all phenomena would likewise possess it.
Yet all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent; all conditions and causes are entirely empty."
"Truly observing a single dharma, one sees that all dharmas have no dual characteristics;
having clearly realized this emptiness, one then perceives all things as empty. He asked:
"Phenomena produced through causes and conditions are themselves the essence and characteristics. He replied: "This is not so."
Why is this? Whether there is a substantial characteristic or no substantial characteristic, neither falls within your reach.

According to what you have said—that a substantial characteristic arises from causes and conditions—since causes and conditions are produced from something else, how can there be a substantial characteristic?
Regarding the essence and characteristics [of phenomena], they arise from their own nature (*svabhāva*) and do not depend on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
If they were dependent upon causes and conditions, they would lack intrinsic nature; for example, that which is borrowed does not belong to oneself.
Therefore, things are formed through conditions and depend upon others; they possess no intrinsic nature.
As the Venerable Nāgārjuna said in verse:
"Phenomena produced by causes and conditions Are themselves devoid of intrinsic nature."
"If there is no intrinsic nature, how can there be an essential characteristic?
[The opponent] asks:
"The essential characteristics of all phenomena are directly perceived by the world."
"How can it be that they do not exist? He replied:
"That is not the case."
The false views of the ignorant and foolish are not to be trusted.

All phenomena subject to arising and ceasing are entirely empty; their arising and ceasing flow so rapidly that they never pause even for a moment. Because they appear as a continuous succession of similar moments, the ignorant perceive them as real, just as one might mistake the successive flickering of a lamp’s flame for a single, constant light. They are like a swift current, a shadow, an echo, a magical illusion, or a mirage.
As the Buddha has taught, both the illusion and the illusionist are entirely non-existent, yet those with deluded vision perceive them as real.
If they were real, hungry ghosts would not see water as fire, nor sand and stones as pus and blood.

However, because sentient beings possess both good and evil, what they perceive follows their respective karma. If there are sentient beings with pure minds and sharp faculties, they are able to see emptiness; for example, yakṣas and hungry ghosts see water from afar, but see fire when they are near it.
He then gave rise to doubt:
"If things possessed reality, there should not be two views.
Because there are two views, one knows they are not real; it is merely due to false perception."
One should know that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics; because they lack intrinsic nature and characteristics, they are entirely without arising or ceasing. Question:
If all phenomena are without arising and without ceasing, how can there be the faults of conceptualizing coming and going, or of annihilationism and eternalism?
Answer: Because one perceives seeds, one conceives of coming and going; if one realizes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), one is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

For example, because there are seeds, there are sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits. One observes the sequence of the sprout's arising, whereby the seed ceases; therefore, it is not annihilated.
Furthermore, because the fruit arises and thus the flower ceases, there is no fault of impermanence.
As the Venerable Deva said in verse:
"When all phenomena exist as a continuum, They are not subject to annihilation."
"Because the cause ceases, the fruit arises; it cannot be called permanent.
For this reason, seeing that causes and conditions are empty is itself the departure from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. Question:
Regarding the statement that "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations," how is one to become free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism?
The answer is:
because of ignorance there are wholesome and unwholesome volitional formations, and so on, up to: because of birth there are old age and death.
Ordinary beings do not understand the continuity of causes and conditions, and thus falsely reckon it to be real.

Because the essence of ignorance is empty, the essence of volitional formations is also empty; continuing in this manner until, because the essence of birth is empty, the essence of old age and death is empty. Since the world exists as a continuity through conventional designations, there is no fault of annihilation; since each moment does not abide, there is no fault of permanence, for ordinary beings die here and are born there in a continuous succession of similar states.

As the Buddha has taught, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) there is no such thing as a sentient being dying here and being born there; it is spoken of only by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through provisional names.

Consciousness is the seed, karmic action is the field, pride is the soil-covering, ignorance is the fertilizer, and the water of craving provides the moisture. Through the conjunction of these various conditions, including the vital essence of the parents, the sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arises. Therefore, name-and-form has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), just as the legs of a bed exist only through mutual dependence for their function.

The first is named kalala; the second, arbuda; the third, peśī; the fourth, ghana; the fifth, praśākhā; and the sixth, sparśa. These stages of the arising of dharmas exist through mutual dependence; they are not called "annihilation."

Because the bodhisattva skillfully understands the dharma of dependent origination, he knows that it is empty; since dependent origination is empty, all dharmas are empty. Because he understands the emptiness of dharmas, he is free from the faults of nihilism and eternalism.
As the Buddha said in a verse within the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*:
"Following conventional designations, one attains all phenomena;
yet within names there is no phenomenon—this is the reality."
For this reason, dharmas do not exist by virtue of verbal expression.
If dharmas existed according to names, then dharmas would possess multiple essences;
yet, as with the dharma of emptiness, there is neither one nor many.
Question: If all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, your statement contains a fault, because they are perceived to exist. Answer:
If a phenomenon were existent, to say it is non-existent would be an error.
Since phenomena are not existent, how can one speak of an error?
For this reason, all phenomena are as they were at the beginning; so too are they at the end.
If all dharmas possessed a fixed, intrinsic nature, they would necessarily be subject to annihilation at the time of final nirvana.
If something were not empty beforehand and is only said to be empty later, this constitutes a false view; it destroys the true Dharma and precludes liberation.
As the Venerable Deva said in verse:
"To see emptiness when it is not empty, one should attain nirvāṇa;
That wrong view is not nirvāṇa—so has the Tathāgata taught."
"Because all dharmas are fundamentally empty, one constantly perceives them as empty; just as the Buddhas of the past perceived the mark of emptiness, so it is now as well.
Therefore, when I say that the dharma of dependent origination is empty, there is no fault in this."

Thus, having first established the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), one subsequently analyzes conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya); regarding the self and sentient beings, the action and the agent, and even identity and difference, there is then no fault.
As the Venerable Nāgārjuna said in verse:
"One who does not speak of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) Does not attain the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
If one does not attain the ultimate truth, Then one cannot attain nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, a verse is spoken:
"The Buddhas, when expounding the Dharma, always rely upon the two truths:
the conventional truth and the ultimate truth."
"If one cannot discern the two noble truths of the ultimate and the conventional, then one will not know the profound meaning of the Buddha-dharma.

Therefore, the emptiness of dependent origination is called suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); this is termed the cultivation of the dhyāna of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
To see that causes and conditions are empty is the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
If one sees emptiness, then one does not perceive the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena; this is called the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).
Because one sees the signless, there is nothing to be wished for; this is called the door of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
Abiding thus in these three doors of liberation, the seed of consciousness no longer gives rise to the sprouts of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) within the triple world.
When consciousness is free from grasping, the suffering of the three realms of existence is extinguished.
Because the three realms of existence are extinguished, one attains the nirvana of quiescence.
As the Venerable Āryadeva said in verse:
"Consciousness has the meaning of a seed, It wanders through the six sense bases;
If one sees that all objects are empty, The sprout of existence is then severed. Question:
The Bodhisattva transcends emptiness and emerges from birth and death; how, then, can they surpass the Śrāvakas?
The answer is:

the Bodhisattva attains both worldly benefits and supramundane benefits. Because they have crossed the *urvī-patha* (the stage of heat), although they are supramundane, they are able to dwell within the world to teach and transform sentient beings.

The śrāvakas are not so; fearing birth and death, they seek swift extinction. Through the supramundane path, they perceive the dharma-realm, and having perceived the dharma-realm, they reach the shore of nirvāṇa.
It is not so for the bodhisattva. Why is this?

Because when the bodhisattva perceives the suffering of sentient beings, they give rise to great compassion; desiring to deliver them, they firmly abide in their adornment and practice the supramundane path for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), perceiving the entire dharma-realm in a single thought-moment.
Having contemplated the dharma-realm, because of their affinity for sentient beings, they do not take up the realization of the fruit, but are instead able to deliver and liberate them.

As the Buddha said in the *Anavatapta-hrada-sūtra*: "For example, suppose two people are about to fall from a mountain peak; one is strong and possesses skillful means. By virtue of those skillful means, although he falls, he rises again and manages to ascend to the mountain peak."
A single person, having little strength and lacking skillful means, remains stuck in retrogression and cannot rise again.
A bodhisattva, however, neither realizes nor clings to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), just as a skilled man reaches the summit of a mountain.
Because śrāvakas cling to the realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are like those with meager skillful means who fall and do not rise.
It is, for example, like an elder who had an only son; due to famine, he traveled far to another country and remained there for many decades.

At a later time, the elder lived in a great city; his family was immensely wealthy, having accumulated vast quantities of pearls and treasures. Gradually gaining employment, he returned to his native country.

The Bodhisattva possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits; having reached the stage of *airyāpathika* (the ground of tranquility) and being oriented toward *nirvāṇa*, he returns to the realm of birth and death out of compassion for sentient beings, enduring diligent suffering for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva mounts the vehicle of great suffering to seek the inconceivable unsurpassed fruit, which transcends all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and is fully endowed with all merit and wisdom; for this reason, he surpasses and crosses over the stage of *urvī*.
What is it for a bodhisattva to mount the vehicle of great suffering?
It is like a person who boards a ship and enters the ocean, encountering a great and violent wind with waves as high as mountains, facing such immeasurable and manifold perils.
The hearts of his companions were filled with anxiety, and they were seized by great terror.
At that time, because the captain skillfully managed the sails, he was able to overcome all perils.
Having crossed over these difficulties, those people of merit and virtue obtained great treasures.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in the ocean of birth and death is likewise thus: hindered by evil associates who do not believe, they tend toward the evil realms.
During the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, they cultivate the practices of purifying the stages and seek pure liberation;
during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, they cultivate the practice of pure meditative concentration.
During the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, one cultivates the practice of pure wisdom, thereby removing the obstacles of the *dūraṅgamā* (Far-reaching) stage.
For this reason, the bodhisattva is said to "ride the vehicle of suffering.

Having fulfilled the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and attained the complete perfection of all unimpeded and unobstructed practices, one realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, through the wisdom of the *dūraṅgamā* stage, one achieves the great fruit.
*Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, Fascicle Upper and Fascicle Lower.
Composed by Bodhisattva Sthiramati.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Daotai and others of the Northern Liang Dynasty. Chapter Two: Critique of Emptiness. Question:

You previously stated that those who ride the Vehicle of Discipline and the Vehicle of Great Suffering attain wondrous fruits and retributions; yet, the realm attained by Bodhisattvas is extremely difficult to comprehend.
The answer is:
The sphere of practice of a bodhisattva is subtle and exceedingly difficult; it can only be accomplished over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayuta kalpas while remaining among ordinary beings, there is no dharma that transcends the world.
As the Venerable Deva said in verse:
"Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, You have always remained on the level of an ordinary person;
You should know now that it shall be the same for the future."
Therefore, the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva is exceedingly vast and likewise difficult to encounter.
It is extremely difficult for distracted sentient beings to hear of it, and even more difficult to explain it; how much more so to actually practice it!
As the Venerable Deva said in verse:
"To be born and encounter the Dharma is difficult; To hear and speak it is likewise difficult.
Though birth and death have no end, Through hearing the Dharma, they do have an end."
He asked: "Venerable One, regarding the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) you previously mentioned, I pray that you will now analyze and explain them for me. What are the ten stages of a bodhisattva?
He replied:

First is the Stage of Joy; second, the Stage Free from Defilement; third, the Stage of Radiance; fourth, the Stage of Blazing Fire; fifth, the Stage Difficult to Conquer; sixth, the Stage of Manifestation; seventh, the Stage of Profundity; eighth, the Immovable Stage; ninth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence; and tenth, the Stage of the Dharma Cloud.
Why is it called the Ground of Joy?
Because one transcends the state of ordinary beings and attains the inconceivable supramundane path, the mind gives rise to joy; therefore, it is named the Ground of Joy.
Why is it called the Ground of Freedom from Defilement?
Because it is free from the defilement of impaired morality, it is called the Ground of Freedom from Defilement.
Why is it called the Ground of Radiance?
Because one attains clear wisdom by relying on the twelve gates of dhyāna, it is called the Ground of Clarity (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*).
Why is it called the Ground of Flames (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*)?

Because one attains the superior awakening-mind and discriminates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), burning the fuel of afflictions so that merit blazes intensely, it is therefore called the Ground of Flames.
Why is it called the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*)?
Because although one cultivates the ten knowledges and subdues the afflictions, one has not yet attained victory; therefore, it is named the Ground Difficult to Conquer.
Why is it called the Ground of Manifestation (*abhimukhī*)?

Because one is able to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, and because the Dharma becomes manifest before one, it is called the Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
Why is it called the Ground of Profundity (*Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*)?

Because one’s love for the Buddha’s merit and wisdom proceeds in succession without interruption by other thoughts, and because one penetrates deeply into the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it is called the Ground of Profundity.
Why is it called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*)?
Because it is free from the signs of form and so forth, and is firm and difficult to shake, it is named the Immovable Ground.
Why is it called the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*)?

Because one enters the four analytical eloquences (*pratisaṃvid*), understands all sounds, and is able to answer every question in a single kṣaṇa, it is called the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
Why is it called the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud?
Because it is able to receive all Buddha-dharmas, just as a great cloud is able to pour down the rain of the Dharma, it is named the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the ten grounds.
These ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the dwelling places where Bodhisattvas abide securely, and they are also able to bring all wisdom to fulfillment,
as is explained in detail in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.

If one can understand the ten stages of the bodhisattva in this way, it is called being skilled in knowing the dwelling places of peaceful abiding; it is also called being skilled in knowing the spheres of the bodhisattva’s vast merits; and it is also able to skillfully know the vast spheres of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merits.
If one cannot understand it in this way, I now make a solemn vow: you should know that such a person has failed to comprehend both the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas and the Dharma of the Tathāgatas.

From the first generation of the resolve until the tenth stage, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly cultivates four practices, as explained in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*: the practice of thoroughly understanding ignorance, the practice of the various pāramitās, the practice of discerning the factors of enlightenment, and the practice of maturing sentient beings.
These four practices are collectively subsumed within two wheels, namely the wheel of merit and the wheel of wisdom.
All the stages of a bodhisattva fully possess these two kinds of fruits: the fruit of wisdom and the fruit of merit.
Question: How does one accomplish the two fruits? Answer:
The fruit of merit of the first stage is to become the king of Jambudvīpa;
the fruit of merit of the second stage is to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) who rules over the four continents;
the fruit of merit of the third stage is to become Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
The fruit of merit of the fourth stage is the sovereignty of the Heavenly King Yama;
the fruit of merit of the fifth stage is the sovereignty of the Heavenly King Tuṣita;
the fruit of merit of the sixth stage is the sovereignty of the Heavenly King Nirmāṇarati.
The fruit of merit of the seventh stage is that of the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations;
the fruit of merit of the eighth stage is that of a Brahmā of a thousand-world system;
the fruit of merit of the ninth stage is that of a Brahmā of a two-thousand-world system.
The fruit of merit of the tenth stage is that of becoming the king of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens within a trichiliocosm, as explained at length in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The resultant fruition of the Tathāgata’s birth and his mastery over the world—this is called the bodhisattva’s wheel of merit.

What is called the "Wisdom Wheel" (*jñānacakra*) of a bodhisattva? At the first stage (*bhūmi*), a bodhisattva, in a single instant, attains one hundred samādhis; beholds the supernormal powers of one hundred Buddhas; can traverse one hundred Buddha-lands; can shake one hundred Buddha-worlds; his radiance universally illumines one hundred Buddha-worlds; can bring one hundred sentient beings to maturity; can know one hundred past kalpas and one hundred future kalpas; can enter one hundred Dharma-gates; can manifest one hundred bodies and yet remain as a single body; and has a retinue adorned by one hundred bodhisattvas.
If by the power of his vows, it exceeds even this by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy;

whether by the power of his body, the power of his radiance, the power of his supernormal faculties, the power of his eyes, the power of his voice, the power of his conduct, the power of his adornments, the power of his sustaining presence, or the power of his liberation—by performing these manifold virtuous deeds, this is called the first-stage bodhisattva accomplishing such immeasurable merit in a single kṣaṇa.
The Bodhisattva dwelling in the second stage attains one thousand samādhis; this is explained in detail as such.
The Bodhisattva dwelling in the third stage attains one hundred thousand samādhis; the rest is also explained in detail as in the case of the first stage.
Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage attain one hundred million samādhis; the rest is as explained in detail for the first stage.
Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage attain one thousand billion samādhis; the rest is also as explained in detail for the first stage.
