A Bodhisattva in the sixth stage attains ten trillion samādhis; the rest is as extensively explained for the first stage.
A Bodhisattva in the seventh stage attains one hundred thousand nayutas of billions of samādhis; the rest is also as extensively explained for the first stage.
A Bodhisattva in the eighth stage attains as many samādhis as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms; the remaining details are as extensively explained for the first stage.

A Bodhisattva in the ninth stage attains as many samādhis as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeyas of ten Buddha-worlds; all other merits are as extensively explained for the first stage.

A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage attains samādhis numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-worlds; all other merits are as extensively described for the first stage.

In a single instant, one may even see Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of billions of Buddha-worlds; just as a Bodhisattva in the first stage sees a hundred Buddha-worlds and brings a hundred sentient beings to maturity in a single instant, so too does a Bodhisattva in the tenth stage.
Question: As the Buddha has taught, no two Buddhas appear in a single world-system.
How is it that a Bodhisattva sees Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably, unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of billions of world-systems?
The answer is:

When the Buddhas state that there are no two Buddhas in a single world-system, they speak for the sake of those sentient beings with dull faculties and small minds, not for the sake of those with sharp faculties and great minds.
As it is stated in your sutra, there are no two wheel-turning sage-kings (*cakravartin*) in a single world-system, nor do two Buddhas appear simultaneously.
However, in reality, there are many wheel-turning sage-kings across the various four-continent worlds (*cāturdvīpaka*), and the appearance of Buddhas in the world is likewise so.
Question: Śākyamuni Buddha is also able to pervade all buddha-fields; why must it be another Buddha? Answer:

If it were as you say, that only a single Buddha could pervade all worlds, then there should not have been the past Great Śākyamuni Buddha nor the appearance of the seven Buddhas who attained perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, my statement that there are many Buddhas is beyond reproach.

Even if the supernatural power of Śākyamuni Buddha were able to pervade all worlds, and if the countless bodhisattvas currently engaged in the extensive cultivation of the ten thousand practices were to fulfill their merits and all attain Buddhahood—there is no possibility that a single person alone could achieve perfect enlightenment while obstructing other bodhisattvas from becoming Buddhas; such a thing cannot exist.

As stated in the *Āgama*, the *Śuṣkavṛkṣa*, the *Dharmacakra*, and other various sūtras: while this sūtra was being preached, sixty bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind, all simultaneously realizing the fruit of arhatship.

It is the same for Bodhisattvas: when their meritorious practices are equal and they attain Buddhahood simultaneously, one should know that there are immeasurable Buddhas throughout the ten directions.

Furthermore, both the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* and the *Āgama* sūtras state that there are Buddhas who have first attained enlightenment, Buddhas who are currently present, and Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, a verse is spoken:
"The immeasurable Buddhas of the past, those of the future as well,
and those who have now attained Buddhahood— all have extinguished sorrow and anxiety."
"All that is honored as the Dharma, Is practiced now in this very life;
In the future it shall be likewise— Such is the Dharma of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Dharmagupta also spoke this verse:
"I prostrate to all Buddhas, To those whose outflows are exhausted, unsurpassed,
The immeasurable bodies of the Buddhas, The Most Victorious Honored Ones who have attained Perfect Enlightenment.
I prostrate to the places where the Perfectly Enlightened Ones were born, And likewise to where they attained Bodhi."
He who was able to turn the wheel of the True Dharma and enter the untainted nirvana;
whether he stood or walked in meditation, or sat as the Tathāgata does,
or lay down like a lion king— I now pay homage to him in every way.
To all the World-Honored Ones above and below, in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
to their Dharma-bodies and their śarīras, I pay homage to all the Buddha-stūpas.
To the Honored Ones among Two-Legged Beings currently dwelling in the east and the north, I pay homage.
Its name is "Invincible," the verse spoken by that Buddha.
If one recites this verse and constantly praises the World-Honored One,
throughout hundreds of kalpas of birth and death, one shall never fall into the evil realms.
As the Buddha said to the Venerable Maudgalyāyana:
"It is not that you have lost your supernormal power; rather, it is Śāriputra who, by means of his own supernormal power, has used his robe-belt to bind the seat of Duṣprasaha."

Since you yourself have made such statements within your own sūtras regarding these Buddhas, how much more so for the Mahāyāna, which elucidates that the Buddhas are immeasurable and boundless, equal to the dharma-realm and identical to the realm of empty space, such that there are Buddhas in every Buddha-world.
The physical conduct of a Bodhisattva on the first stage is pure; although they possess fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana*), these cannot disturb them.
A Bodhisattva at the seventh dwelling is neither said to have severed the fetters nor said to possess them.
What is meant by "not having fetters yet not severing fetters"?
Because one is not disturbed by the afflictions of the fetters, it is called "being without fetters"; because one cherishes the Buddha’s merits, it is called "having fetters."

Upon completing the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he attains the eighth stage; all practices are fully perfected such that there is nothing further to be done, and because all fetters and afflictions are exhausted, he realizes bodhi. Abiding in a state of empty stillness, he attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), just like an arhat.

Having thus attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), if the Buddhas do not exhort and entreat them, they would immediately enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* within that very meditative concentration.
As it is said in the sūtras, those who attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena are free from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), just like arhats.
They attain the nirvana without remainder, depart from birth and death, and obtain the ten masteries (*vaśitā*).
What are these ten? They are:

mastery over lifespan, mastery over the mind, mastery over requisites, mastery over karma, mastery over the place of birth, mastery over liberation, mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), mastery over vows, mastery over phenomena (*dharma*), and mastery over wisdom (*jñāna*).
Having attained such mastery through the excellent cultivation of the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda),
he subdues the four māras. What are these four?
The māra of the aggregates, the māra of afflictions, the māra of death, and the celestial māra—
for the sake of sentient beings, he renders them all of one single flavor and attains objectless compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*).
Like a wish-fulfilling medicinal tree, he causes all the aspirations of sentient beings to be fulfilled according to their wishes.
Question: How is it that the karmic actions performed by a bodhisattva himself can cause sentient beings to obtain their wishes according to their aspirations? Answer:
The Bodhisattva takes compassion as his essence; just as seeing a venomous snake can kill a person, sentient beings obtain benefit simply by seeing the Bodhisattva.
Question: Since a Bodhisattva in the eighth stage has exhausted all fetters (saṃyojana), why did the Bodhisattva in his final birth give rise to Rāhula?
The answer is:
It is indeed as you have said.
If a bodhisattva in his final existence were to possess actual desire, then even a Buddha could not be attained, let alone Rāhula.
Question: How can there be no Buddha? Answer:
If one violates the precepts, there is no *śīlapāramitā*. If there is no *śīlapāramitā*, then there are no *pāramitās* at all.

As the Buddha has said: if there is no morality, there is no giving; if there is no giving, there is no patience; if there is no patience, there is no vigor; if there is no vigor, there is no meditative concentration; if there is no meditative concentration, there is no wisdom; if there is no wisdom, there are no merits whatsoever; if there are no merits whatsoever, there is no Buddha; and if there is no Buddha, there is no Rāhula.
Why do you doubt whether Rāhula was born with fetters or without them?

A Bodhisattva dwelling in the eighth stage is free from all afflictions, just like an Arhat; yet, by the power of skillful means, he manifests the enjoyment of the five desires and commits various transgressions, renouncing his status as a Wheel-Turning King over the four continents in order to cause sentient beings to develop a mind of weary detachment.
It is just as the bhikṣu Śāriputra spoke in the verses on the Buddha’s past conduct:
“Manifesting one body as many bodies, Having performed this, it is most excellent;
Neither real nor unreal, Each and every one brings joy.”
Laxity gives rise to sensual desire; the vigor of youth is confounded by madness.
To manifest the practice of desire and lead others to the further shore—meditative wisdom can burn away and extinguish all fetters of the realm of desire.
"The fetters of desire are exceedingly wild and unruly; [the Bodhisattva] can manifest his mind accordingly.

The Bodhisattva contemplates desire as being like an illusion or a dream; for this reason, he causes them to turn their minds away from it, employing the great compassionate Bodhisattva’s various illusory arts to transform their hearts.
Question: How does one perform such magical illusions to delude sentient beings? Answer:
The Bodhisattva constantly employs the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) as skillful methods to teach and transform all sentient beings.
He acts in concert with them for their benefit in order to destroy their fetters (*saṃyojana*).
This is like the causal conditions of the former life of the Bodhisattva Śikhī: with a mind crazed by desire, he carried a corpse on his shoulders while running, shouting, singing, and dancing.

The skillful means of a bodhisattva likewise manifest conformity with them; for the sake of removing the suffering of intense desire in that woman, he manifests the same activities, yet this is not called false speech.
All such "sameness of activity" through the skillful means of bodhisattvas is never false speech.

Worldly magical arts provide little benefit; however, when a bodhisattva attains the gate of the illusion-like samādhi of immeasurable liberation, all that they do can greatly benefit and bring accomplishment to sentient beings, and thus there is no fault.
Question: Is Rāhula an emanation or is he real? Answer:
Neither of the two positions is erroneous.
The body of a bodhisattva is itself a celestial body.
As stated in the *Benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Arising), the Buddha told Ānanda:
The Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of sentient beings; he does not turn the wheel of Dharma with a celestial body.
Why is this? Because he wishes to cause sentient beings to be free from indolence.
The Buddha attained perfect enlightenment by means of his celestial body; it is not something that can be achieved by us ordinary worldlings.
For this reason, the God among Gods, out of compassion for sentient beings, manifests in the world with parents, wife, children, and kinsmen.
If Rāhula is currently present as a magical creation, there is no fault in this;
if he is a real person, there is likewise no fault.

The Bodhisattva, having attained inconceivable liberation through skillful means and dwelling on the stages (bhūmi), brings sentient beings to maturity, acting as mutual parents, siblings, wives, and children for one another.
Question: Is Rāhula a bodhisattva? Answer:

Not only is Rāhula alone a bodhisattva; all the young Śākya princes dwelling in the city of Kapilavastu—Ānanda, Nanda, Devadatta, Aniruddha, and the others—are likewise bodhisattvas of great power who have reached the stage of non-retrogression.
As stated in the verse from the *Brahmāyuḥ-sūtra*:
"Whether he be a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa) or an emanation of the Buddha,
Devadatta is the companion of the Great Sage."
Or again, they may become father and son, Constantly acting as intimate family members;
The Bodhisattva possesses great power, Able to perform such through skillful transformation.
Together with the Buddha and other people, As well as the various great sages, the Bodhisattvas—
Ānanda, Nanda, and others, Aniruddha, Śāriputra,
Bhadrika and Kapphiṇa, Upāli and the rest— Acting as father and sons,
kinsmen and retinue, They all gathered together to surround him.
Question: Devadatta was constantly a great enemy of the Bodhisattva throughout five hundred lifetimes;
why, then, is he also called a bodhisattva?
Answer: Is Devadatta not an enemy of the Buddha? Why is this so?

If Devadatta were an enemy of the Buddha, and while the Bodhisattva cultivated goodness, Devadatta constantly committed various evils, how could they meet and encounter one another together in every successive life?
For this reason, Devadatta is not an enemy of the Bodhisattva.

It is like two people traveling in opposite directions—one toward the east and one toward the west—where they grow further apart with every step and remain constantly at odds; how could they ever be companions or meet one another?
If Devadatta were an enemy of the Bodhisattva, then the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, would have a great fault.
[The interlocutor] asks:
What fault would there be?
The answer is:

If that were so, the Buddha would not be omniscient, nor would he possess supernormal powers; he would be deluded and thus unable to protect sentient beings. He would not possess a vajra-body, and the Tathāgata would consequently have residual karma that he could not exhaust.
How is it known that the Buddha is not omniscient?
While the Tathāgata was on Vulture Peak Mountain, he was not aware when he was crushed by a rock thrown by Devadatta; therefore, one should know that the Tathāgata is not omniscient.
What is meant by "lacking supernormal power"?
Devadatta struck [the Buddha] with a mallet to cause him harm, yet he could not be restrained; by this one should know that he lacks supernormal power.
What is meant by "delusion"?
It refers to seeing harm approaching and failing to know how to avoid it; therefore, one should know that this constitutes delusion.
What is meant by "being unable to protect sentient beings"?
Devadatta committed the five heinous crimes and was not saved; by this one should know that he was unable to protect sentient beings.
Why is it called "not a vajra-body"?

Even a Wheel-Turning Sage King, with his meager karmic rewards, is free from harm and malice; how much more so for the Tathāgata, the King who turns the Wheel of Dharma? That his body bled when crushed by a stone shows that the Tathāgata does not possess a vajra-body.
What is meant by "having residual karma that cannot be completely exhausted"?
When one is struck by another, it should be understood that the Tathāgata’s residual karma is not yet exhausted.
If one wishes for the Buddha to be free from such faults, the Tathāgata should have utterly extinguished all enemies.

It is solely through skillful means that he wishes to cause sentient beings to give rise to a mind of revulsion; thus, he manifests the commission of parricide and falls into hell, desiring to demonstrate that the retribution of karma cannot be destroyed.
Furthermore, for the sake of those who are about to fall into hell, one takes refuge in the Tathāgata and requests the Buddha to provide protection.

Moreover, so that noble and wealthy persons of future generations may enter the Buddha-dharma, [the Buddha manifests this] lest they, relying on their own power and influence, should further strike others with whips and staves, causing these sentient beings to think:
"If even the body of the Tathāgata can be harmed and destroyed, how much more so for an ordinary person like me, one of meager merit?"
Regarding what you said about the heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), these are merely the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.
Although such heinous crimes are nominally five, in reality there are two:
schisming the Sangha and harming the Buddha; such karmic acts do not exist in the world.
Devadatta was the Bodhisattva Mahāpiṅgala; in order to prevent sentient beings from committing the crime of parricide, he manifested the performance of two karmic acts and fell into hell.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas transform sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them, even manifesting deeds identical to those of Māra, thereby causing Māra Pāpīyas to display the three celestial maidens as manifestations of the Tathāgata’s sign of desirelessness.

Furthermore, a rain of swords, blades, spears, and lances fell, manifesting the Tathāgata’s characteristic of being free from anger, as well as his freedom from the characteristics of craving and delusion.
A question was asked:
"The intention of the celestial Māra in coming was to destroy the Tathāgata’s mind of perfect enlightenment."
How can you say that [this teaching] is intended to reveal that the Tathāgata is free from greed and hatred?
The answer is:
it is not for the purpose of negation.

Why is this? If even when a Tathāgata has transcended the realm of Māra, he were still obstructed by Māra, then since the Great Brahmā King has also transcended the realm of Māra, why does he not likewise obstruct awakening?
This is the wondrous fruit of the Way; it can neither be taken away by anyone nor bestowed by anyone, and is therefore indestructible.
As for the mention of Māra’s disturbances, there are generally two meanings.
What are these two?
First, there are those who actually possess evil karma and are disturbed by Māra;

second, there are those who, in order to advance new learners and make their minds firm, are subjected to the harassment and trials of Māra—yet these are actually true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) of the Bodhisattva appearing as Māra to increase their merit and virtue.
It is like a traveler on a road who crosses a perilous and difficult pass quickly out of fear;
or like a fine ox that becomes well-trained and useful with only a light whip. Question:
"Are there also Māras who are bodhisattvas?
He replied:
"It is not only the Māras of this world who are bodhisattvas; most of the Māra kings throughout the worlds of the ten directions are bodhisattvas."
As stated in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, those who act as Māras in the worlds of the ten directions are for the most part bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation.
Those who are able to beg for their hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, and brain—those who speak such words are all bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation. Why is this?
Were it not for the Bodhisattvas, they would not be capable of such a task.
It is like a fragrant elephant treading upon something that is beyond the reach of a donkey; only the Bodhisattvas are able to perform it.

As explained at length therein, for this reason one should know that a bodhisattva skillfully understands the various conducts of sentient beings; desiring to manifest their power of merit, wisdom, and skillful means, they may appear to commit murder or act as a beggar.
Question: If Rāhula is truly a bodhisattva, why is he further called a śrāvaka arhat? Answer:
A bodhisattva is also called a śrāvaka and is also called an arhat.
Why is this? Because they cause all sentient beings to hear of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are therefore called śrāvakas.
Because they are worthy of receiving offerings from all devas, humans, and asuras, they are called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
For the sake of transforming sentient beings, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas manifest as Śrāvaka Arhats.
Question: Are all other śrāvakas also bodhisattvas? Answer:
There are also other śrāvakas who are bodhisattvas; as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the five hundred disciples such as Śāriputra were all bodhisattvas, and all shall become buddhas.
All śrāvakas are in fact avaivartika bodhisattvas, as is explained in detail in the *Avaivartikadharmacakrasūtra*.
For this reason, one should know that bodhisattvas all manifest as śrāvakas.
Question: Do all śrāvakas attain Buddhahood? Answer:
That a śrāvaka attains Buddhahood is likewise without fault.
Question: In what way is it without fault?

Answer: First one cuts off the hindrance of the fetters (*saṃyojana-āvaraṇa*), and subsequently one cuts off the hindrance to knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*); having purified the stages (*bhūmi*), one proceeds toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Therefore, there is no fault. Question:
Having burned away the fetters and latent tendencies, they are like parched grain sprouts.
How, then, can one become a Buddha?
The answer is:
If it were as you say— that one cannot attain Buddhahood because the fetters and afflictions have been severed—
then you and all sentient beings, who possess all these afflictions, would already be Buddhas.
If you think that one who possesses afflictions is not a Buddha, then one who is free from afflictions should be a Buddha.

Your claim that burning away the fetters of affliction is like scorching the sprouts of grain so that they do not become a Buddha is also impossible; I do not intend for the seeds of affliction to give rise to the sprouts of the Buddha-dharma.
Because you are deluded, lacking wisdom, and possess perverted understanding, you claim that afflictions are the seeds of the Buddha-dharma.
In reality, an Arhat first abandons the afflictions and subsequently eliminates the cognitive obstructions; by cultivating the path to Bodhi, they attain Perfect Enlightenment.

Among the arhats, some have partially severed the cognitive hindrances while others have not; some have attained the samādhi of non-contention while others have not; some have attained the five supernormal powers while others have not; some have attained the four analytical knowledges while others have not; and some have attained mastery over entering and emerging from dhyāna while others have not.
Why is this? Because all obstructions to omniscience have not been severed. Question:
What is called the obstruction to knowledge?
The answer is:
supramundane ignorance is called the obstruction to knowledge.
As it is said in a verse from the *Śālistamba-sūtra*:
"Ignorance is of two kinds: Worldly and supramundane.
The worldly ignorance and formations Have already been abandoned by the noble ones."
Foolish and lacking sublime understanding, they cannot know things as they truly are;
relying upon this mind-consciousness, they remain in the perilous places of the dharma-realm.
Having failed to reach the fundamental source, how can they emerge with certainty?
"The Dharma-body realizes nirvāṇa; only a Buddha can fully comprehend it.

Thus, the Buddha, the Bhagavān, alone is able to know its essential nature, wisdom, and the great compassion that severs the fetters; this is what is called the obstruction to knowledge severed by the śrāvakas.
There are two kinds of śrāvakas: first, those who diligently cultivate meditative concentration, who are persons of dull faculties;
second, those who dedicate themselves toward bodhi and are able to sever the cognitive obscurations, who are persons of sharp faculties.
Regarding those who delight in practicing dhyāna, as stated in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra*, they are like ordinary crystal that can never become a maṇi jewel;
likewise, the śrāvakas’ cultivation of dhyāna can never result in the fruit of bodhi.
This is the realm of all Buddhas, not something known by me.
Whether there is one vehicle or many vehicles, I have now briefly set forth their meaning merely to clarify that the Buddha's teachings do not contradict one another.
I have not yet understood this.
It is like a wealthy householder who, having traveled far and become utterly exhausted, manifests a conjured city.
This sutra states that there is only the One Vehicle; in reality, there are no three.
The Buddha himself has also declared that there is only one vehicle (ekayāna), and no second or third. Question:
By what practice did the Tathāgata sever the fetters and afflictions (saṃyojana-kleśa) to attain Buddhahood?
Answer: It is stated in the sutras that the Buddha told Ānanda:
"One who is able to cultivate the four bases of psychic power can remain for one kalpa or for many kalpas, until the end of birth and death."
All the sutras speak in this same way.
If you say that there are no afflictions, I also say the same.
If there are those who love me and place their faith and refuge in me, I shall explain it for you.
Question: How does one abide in life? Answer:

Arhats are free from afflictions and are equal to Bodhisattvas dwelling in the eighth stage; because they have skillfully cultivated the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), they are able to remain in the world at will, even until the end of birth and death.
Rāhula, Piṇḍola, and the others all remain in the world; do they remain by means of this very body, or do they remain by means of other bodies?
If they remained in the world by means of their actual physical bodies, then that would be impossible.
If a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) were to remain for many kalpas, such a thing is possible.

It is also as described in the *Saṃghīti-sūtra*, where it says that Tathāgatas such as Nīlanetra, for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas, remained in the Ābhāsvara Heaven together with a multitude of śrāvakas for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, just as the śrāvakas in that heaven abide for many kalpas.
It should be known that within this realm there are also śrāvakas who are able to abide in such a manner.

Just as there are śrāvakas without fetters who are able to abide in such a manner, it should be known that bodhisattvas of the eighth stage are likewise able to abide thus, having exhausted birth and death.
Question: The Buddha stated that Maitreya Bodhisattva is in his "last birth before Buddhahood" (ekajātipratibaddha).
On this basis, should it be understood that bodhisattvas undergo birth?
How is it that one obtains the name "unborn"?
The answer is:
To speak of "arising" is a phenomenon of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas manifest birth through the power of skillful means; it is not ultimately real.
As Vimalakīrti said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"Since no birth can be apprehended, how can the Tathāgata bestow upon you, O Noble One, the prediction that after one more life you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Is it birth in the past, birth in the future, or birth in the present?
If it is birth in the past, that past birth has already ceased.
As for birth in the future, that future birth has not yet arrived.
Present birth, likewise, has no abiding.

Just as one observes that past, future, and present births are all unattainable, for this reason I say that a Bodhisattva in the eighth stage, having completed all conditioned practices during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, abides in unconditioned practice. This is like an Arhat who, having severed the fetters and proclivities, speaks this verse:
"From the first generation of the mind, Through skillful means, I have practiced the various stages."
"Having attained the eighth stage, One attains mastery and exhausts all fetters.
Chapter Three: Cultivating All Practices in Accordance with the Path Question:

As previously stated, a Bodhisattva in the eighth stage thoroughly severs the afflictions and all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). How then does one become a Buddha and attain omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)?
The answer is:

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva eliminates all evils of the body, brings the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to cessation, and, being detached from birth and death, sports with sovereign mastery. The Vajra-wielding Māras constantly follow, protect, and assist him, and he attains the pure Vajra-body, as is explained in detail in the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*.

Attaining the wisdom of the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), they purify the ninth stage; among two thousand Brahmās, they attain sovereign power, are able to skillfully expound the Dharma as great Dharma-preachers, and are able to enter the secret treasury of the Tathāgatas.

He purifies the tenth stage, attains immeasurable and boundless incantations and arts, and is able to bring all things under his sovereign and unimpeded control; he becomes the celestial son Maheśvara and likewise serves as the refuge for all worlds.
Question: As for what is called Maheśvara, is he the same as the Maheśvara of the world, or is there some difference? Answer:
This is the sovereign of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, not the worldly sovereign.
As for what you call Maheśvara, although the name is the same, the persons are not one and the same; there is the Maheśvara of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and there is the Piśāca Maheśvara.

As for those in the Pure Abodes, such Bodhisattvas are adjacent to the stage of Buddhahood, separated by it only as if by a thin veil; in a single kṣaṇa, they are able to fully comprehend all dharmas as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions, and they can cause all the worlds of the ten directions to tremble violently by blowing with their mouths.

Furthermore, with a single body, he pervades all Buddha-lands; it is just as when a crown prince first assumes his office, through the power of his own karma, a great precious lotus flower spontaneously appears by transformation. He receives the station of the knowledge of all modes and sits upon the king’s throne of precious lotuses, surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas who likewise sit upon lotus flowers.

Once seated upon the precious lotus flower, the Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions emit great rays of light that illuminate this Bodhisattva as they receive the position of consecration, just as when the eldest son of a Cakravartin King receives the royal throne.

Having received the empowerment, they immediately, upon that very seat, severed the subtle obstacles regarding the sphere of wisdom and attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Vairocana Samādhi, and the Lotus Samādhi; they attained the Samādhi of Certainty in All Real Dharmas, the Samādhi of Inconceivable Liberation, the Samādhi of the Deep and Fearless Ocean-Waters, the Subtle, Pure, and Stainless Samādhi, the Samādhi of the Equality of All Dharmas Beyond Speech, and even the Vajra Samādhi.
Having attained these various samādhis, being entirely without obstruction and fulfilling all practices, they awaken to the realm of omniscience and realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having attained perfect enlightenment, they obtain the ten powers of a Tathāgata;
they obtain the fourfold analytical knowledge and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, enabling them to reach all Buddha-lands;
they obtain the indestructible Dharma-body of all Buddhas, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
All characteristics of the actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely extinguished;
one attains the state of unconditioned tranquility.

There are two causes and conditions for ascending to the stage of the Tathāgata: first, manifesting a form-body throughout all worlds, entirely through the power of effortless action resulting from original vows.
Second, because sentient beings have diverse conceptualizations, the Tathāgata is able to manifest various forms and images in accordance with them all;
this is called the Tathāgata’s unimpeded Dharma-body.
Question: As it is said in the sutras, one who is able to abide in the Buddha-dharma from the moment of initial renunciation is called the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Answer:
This is not so. If you take this name to be the Dharma-body, such that there is only the Dharma and no Buddha, then the Three Refuges would not exist.

If you wish to establish the complete Three Refuges, then from the first stage up to the tenth stage, when one attains perfect enlightenment in the Pure Abodes, the sovereign and responsive transformation body is called the Dharma-body, and it is fully endowed with the Triple Gem.
Question: If the Dharma-body is designated by such names, it is deceptive and lacks reality. Why is this so?
The Tathāgata, fully endowed with merit, departed from Tuṣita Heaven and descended to Jambudvīpa to be born in a royal palace, where, in his final body, he attained the realization of Bodhi.
Why is it said that one attains the Buddha-way in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and this is called the Dharmakāya?
The answer is:
Buddhahood is not attained in Jambudvīpa; the merits of the ten stages are not dharmas of the Desire Realm, much less is perfect enlightenment attained in Jambudvīpa.

Did I not previously state that a Bodhisattva in the eighth stage, having exhausted all fetters and outflows, can become a Brahmā king of a thousand-world system; a Bodhisattva in the ninth stage becomes a Brahmā king of two thousand worlds; and a Bodhisattva in the tenth stage becomes a Brahmā king of a trichiliocosm?
It is possible for one to be born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens by the power of their vow;
however, it is not the case that they could attain Buddhahood with a physical body in Jambudvīpa.
For this reason, one should know that it is the Śuddhāvāsa deities who attain Buddhahood, not those of Jambudvīpa.
It is asked:
Even if one were born in Jambudvīpa and attained Buddhahood, would they not likewise be able to attain mastery over the trichiliocosm?
Answer: This is not so. Why is that?
The retribution of merit and virtue certainly has its place; it is because you do not know this that you speak in such a manner.
If Śākyamuni Buddha, having been born in Jambudvīpa, attained mastery over the trichiliocosm, he must likewise have attained mastery over all worlds in the ten directions.
Question: Even if one were to bring all the ten directions under one's control, what further fault would there be? Answer:
If that were so, there would be only a single Buddha-world, and the Buddhas of the ten directions would have no basis for their fruition.
Furthermore, as stated in various sutras, it is said that Śākyamuni Tathāgata reigns over the trichiliocosm, but it is not said that he reigns over worlds throughout the ten directions.
If it were as you say, then there would be no cause and effect.
As it is stated in the sutras, when the Buddhas appear in the world, the lands and the sentient beings therein are all *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive supports), each having its own fixed limits.
Therefore, you should know that it was in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens that he attained perfect enlightenment and took charge of the trichiliocosm, not in Jambudvīpa. Question:
If the Buddha did not attain perfect enlightenment in Jambudvīpa, then the four stūpas of the Tathāgata would be of no benefit.
The answer is:
Have I not already stated this?

If one receives a body due to the causes and conditions of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), then there is no attainment of the Way and no *śīlapāramitā*. If there is no *śīlapāramitā*, then there are no *pāramitās*; if there are no *pāramitās*, then there is no Buddha; and if there is no Buddha, then there are no four reliquaries (*caitya*).
Question: What you have said is entirely contrary to reason. Why is this so?
All the masters of the various schools maintain that all Buddhas emerge from Jambudvīpa.

Thus, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was born in the Lumbinī Garden; he attained perfect enlightenment at the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) in the city of Gayā; he turned the wheel of Dharma in Vārāṇasī; and he entered parinirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara.
Therefore, what you have said is incorrect. He replied: "This is not so."
Why is this? It is because it is not my intention that the Tathāgatas should emerge from here [this world] to attain perfect enlightenment in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
If they were to attain perfect enlightenment in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, there would be no birth in a royal palace, nor would there be renunciation, nor would there be the realization of the Way.
Why is this? If that were so, the Tathāgata would have no kinsmen, nor would he have a place of birth, nor would there be any cessation.
As extensively explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Jñānaprasthāna-sūtra*, and the *Tathāgatotpatti-sambhava-sūtra*, the Tathāgata is neither born nor does he cease.
Kāśyapa himself also declared, "I have gone forth in reliance upon the knowledge of all modes.
One should know that this meaning demonstrates the non-arising of the Tathāgata;
when he extended his foot from within the golden coffin and Kāśyapa paid him homage, it clarified that the Tathāgata does not perish.
Therefore, one should know that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is neither born nor extinguished.
Question: Is it the case that the Tathāgata has not even the slightest birth or extinction?
Answer: I now explain according to principle that the Tathāgata truly has neither birth nor extinction; this is not a falsehood.
The Tathāgata merely manifests birth and extinction through skillful means, all of which are inconceivable, for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
As the Buddha said in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "If I were to manifest my true body in this Sahā world, not a single person would receive my transformation."

Therefore, this place is most profound; it is both secret and yet called manifest. This is because sentient beings of inferior faculties possess shallow wisdom and are unable to understand the most profound Dharma; for their sake, these matters are thus manifested through skillful means.
He spoke in verse:
“The Mahāyāna is profound and vast; It is manifest and easy to explain.
Yet those of dull intellect and narrow minds Conceive fear and doubt upon hearing it.”
Those who are true sons of the Buddha can know its profound depth;
now I speak this truly for those who seek Buddhahood.
Those who have achieved the two vehicles, as well as humans and devas of keen faculties—
Receiving blessings by means of this vehicle—this is called the path of the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāyāna is able to give birth to the paths of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
if one obstructs the Mahāyāna, how can one attain any of the fruits?
Just as all letters depend on their basic forms, and without those bases there would be no letters,
so too, apart from the Mahāyāna, there would be no vehicles at all.
Those of dull faculties and little wisdom do not believe in the Mahāyāna.
Because one cannot believe [in it], there would be no vehicle at all.
That which benefits oneself while simultaneously benefiting others is called the Unsurpassed Vehicle (anuttarayāna);
therefore, one should draw near to it until the path of Buddhahood is attained.
"This meaning is extremely profound and difficult to manifest; it should not be explained to people everywhere.
[The interlocutor] asks:
"Even if it should not be taught in all places, it ought to be explained to those who are capable of understanding it."
If one has resolved upon the Great Mind and increases wisdom, for such a person, one should provide a full and detailed exposition as previously described.
The answer is:

there are four inconceivables, namely, the inconceivability of the Buddha, the inconceivability of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the inconceivability of nāgas and spirits, and the inconceivability of karmic retribution.

The Buddha’s inconceivable dharma of manifestation is intended solely for sentient beings of sharp faculties, who are fully capable of receiving all the dharmas taught since the time of Vairocana Buddha.
Question: How did one come to receive [the teaching] from that Buddha in succession down to the present day? Answer:
The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata employs four skillful means (*upāya*) for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

What are these four? First, *tattvārtha-pratibhidi*; second, *tattvanirukti-prativedha*; third, *adhyātma-prativedha*; and fourth, *adhyātmanirukti-prativedha*. These four are profound and subtle; since there is no way to translate them into the language of Qin, their Sanskrit originals have been preserved as they are.
Question: If the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is eternally quiescent, signless, and unconditioned, how can it accord with that which possesses signs? Answer:

By the power of their original vows, they are like a bhikṣu who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti); although he lacks mental activity, because of his prior resolve, if the sound of a ghaṇṭā is struck and reaches his ears, he immediately emerges from that absorption as soon as the sound arises.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: having generated the bodhicitta through the power of his original vow, even though at the time he attains the dharma-body of quiescence his mind and consciousness are signless, he still teaches and transforms sentient beings by virtue of the power of non-action.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s signless Dharma-body is able to universally respond to and accord with that which possesses signs.
Thus, in the ten billion Tuṣita heavens and the ten billion Yāma heavens within the trichiliocosm, he simultaneously manifests his form-body in all of them.
Having manifested his form-body, he may either relinquish his life-span, or manifest entering the womb, or manifest his initial birth,
or act as an attendant to Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others; or manifest walking seven steps, or manifest the lion’s roar,
or further declare himself to be the most honored and supreme among gods and humans, and finally...
The final body severs birth, old age, sickness, and death; it may manifest as a youth,
or manifest entering the palace, or manifest leaving home, or manifest practicing austerities, or manifest sitting at the site of enlightenment,
or manifest subduing Māra, or manifest first attaining Buddhahood, or manifest awakening sentient beings, or manifest having long since attained Buddhahood, or manifest...
He manifests being entreated by Śakra and Brahmā to turn the wheel of Dharma; he manifests bringing to maturity those sentient beings who are not yet matured;
he manifests delivering those already matured; he manifests about to enter nirvāṇa; he manifests having already entered nirvāṇa;
he manifests the entire-body relics and the divided-body relics in Jambudvīpa; or he manifests descending from Tuṣita.
Even unto manifesting the liberation and maturation of sentient beings, he manifests forms according to what is appropriate for them to see—
whether appearing repeatedly or appearing only for a brief duration.
If this is what is taught, it is called the true meaning.
How could one who has practiced the various pāramitās for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas ever have their fruit utterly extinguished within forty or fifty years?
How can it be said that the cause is like Mount Sumeru or Mount Cakravāḍa, while the fruit is but a tiny fraction of a mustard seed or a mote of dust?
Therefore, what you have stated is a contradiction.
In my Dharma, it is possible for the cause to be like a mustard seed while the fruit is like Mount Sumeru, the Great Mountain; this accords with this principle.

Therefore, through causes spanning three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one attains the exhaustion of all fruits of birth and death, yet the *dharmakāya* remains eternally present to manifest and transform sentient beings, as clarified in the "Life Span" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and as also taught in the "Chapter on the Prophecy of Mañjuśrī."
What is meant by the *dhāraṇī* called "The Many" (*bahudhāraṇī*)?
As the Buddha has said:
"I have completed my buddha-work."
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived.
In this same way, the Buddhas of the ten directions also speak these words in order to transform sentient beings; yet in reality, they do not pass away.
The supernatural transformations and manifestations of all Buddha-lands are entirely equal to empty space and the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, one should know that the Dharma-body is eternal, whereas the form-body is impermanent because it is a response-transformation.
If one views the Buddha by means of the physical body, this is not called seeing the Tathāgata.
As the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If one sees the Buddha by means of form, Or seeks the Tathāgata through sound,..."
"Such a person walks a deviant path and cannot be said to see the Buddha.
For this reason, to contemplate the Buddha by means of the Dharma-body is called truly seeing the Tathāgata.
When the bhikṣuṇī Padmā saw the Buddha’s physical body, she thought to herself:
"I am the very first to see the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You did not see me previously;
it was only Subhūti who, through his realization of the Dharma-body, has already seen me.
Therefore, you should know that those who have attained the rank of the Ten Abodes are said to 'see the Dharma-body.'"
If one pays homage to the Dharma-body, one pays homage to all form-bodies (rūpakāya).

As the Buddha said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, if a person invokes the name and makes offerings to the Dharma-body of Avalokiteśvara, it is superior to making offerings to the form-bodies of sixty-two billion Buddhas.
Why is this? Because one who has attained the rank of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) realizes the Buddha’s Dharma-body; such a person is called both a bodhisattva and a Buddha.
Therefore, it should be known that the Dharma-body is the fundamental basis, and all immeasurable form-bodies (rūpakāya) are manifested and brought forth in reliance upon the Dharma-body.
Therefore, the Buddha provisionally taught that the physical bodies (rūpakāya) equaling sixty-two billion Ganges-sands are not as good as making offerings to a single Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
As the Buddha said in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*: "In this way, Kāśyapa!"
It is like people in the world who pay respectful homage when the moon first appears, yet do not show such respect when it has reached its fullness.
Why is this? Because [the moon] has proceeded from its beginning until its completion.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
If a son of good family wishes to pay respect to me, he should first pay homage to the bodhisattvas. Why is this?
Because the Buddha attained fulfillment while on the bodhisattva stages, he continues to manifest through the transformations of birth and death in various forms to benefit sentient beings.
For this reason, it is truly said that he has already attained the fruit of Buddhahood; this is the Buddha’s actual teaching and not a falsehood.
Question: If one has not yet entered the bodhisattva stages, may a bhikṣu who has received full ordination pay him homage? Answer:
One should pay homage [to them], because a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind to attain enlightenment surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
As the Venerable Rāhula said in verse:
"If one resolves with a profound mind, Enlightenment will surely arise; Therefore, for the sake of all..."
"who are worthy of our reverence. He asked:
"How can a bhikṣu who has received full ordination pay homage to a bodhisattva who has not yet received full ordination and has not yet entered the stage of certainty?"
Answer: One should pay homage to the bodhisattva. Why is this?
The precepts of the śrāvakas must necessarily be abandoned once one’s entire lifespan has ended;

however, the bodhisattva, having resolved upon the mind of awakening, achieves the natural, ultimate, and liberative precepts. Therefore, even though a śrāvaka has received full ordination, they should still pay homage to a bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stage of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma).

Because the essential nature of a bodhisattva is non-killing and free from the use of weapons and staves, they possess a sense of shame and remorse such that they harbor no intent to kill even an insect or an ant.
Thus it is explained at length: their essential nature is non-stealing, and so on, up to their essential nature being free from wrong views.
Just as the prātimokṣa precepts are relinquished at the time of death or when one abandons the religious life,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva achieves the precepts of nature (dharmatā-śīla) and never relinquishes them midway until reaching the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
For this reason, although they have received the full precepts, one should nevertheless pay them homage. Question:
One who has perfected the nature of the precepts is worthy of offerings, but should not be prostrated to.
The answer is: Not so.
Because they possess the merit of the precepts, they too should be venerated; how could it be merely a matter of making offerings?

Regarding your statement that one should not pay homage to a bodhisattva who has not received the precepts, I shall now further explain this to you in detail: it is not solely by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) that one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*).
As stated in the *Vinayavibhāṣā*, there are ten ways of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the bodhisattva has various ways of receiving the precepts.
What are these ten?
As when the Buddha himself said, "Welcome, bhikṣu," and [the person] naturally attained full ordination, as in the case of Mahākāśyapa;
or as when one received full ordination through the causal condition of a self-vow, as in the case of Kauṇḍinya.
One may receive full ordination through the realization of the Truths, as in the case of the bhikṣuṇī Prajāpatī;
or one may receive full ordination by means of the eight rules, as in the case of the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā.
Receiving full ordination by dispatching a messenger, as in the case of the śrāmaṇera Sudānīya;
receiving full ordination through a formal debate on doctrine, as in the case of the bhikṣu Yaśas and others;
and receiving full ordination by the "Come hither" formula, as in the case of Bhadrapāla.
The full ordination (upasampadā) may be received through the three refuges, as in the case of receiving the full ordination from a fifth preceptor in a border region;
otherwise, in the central lands, the full ordination is received through the formal ritual of the white-fourfold motion (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
For this reason, a bodhisattva always maintains the full precepts and never abandons them.
Question: If one is clad in the dharma robes, may a bodhisattva pay homage to a lay bodhisattva?
The answer is:

The Bodhisattva, fully endowed with the five supernormal powers through skillful means, conforms to all the physical forms of sentient beings and adopts their dress; likewise, he follows all sentient beings as they enter the various realms of existence, assuming their respective appearances.
The great bodhisattvas and others assume transformed bodies in accordance with the karmic retributions of sentient beings, as stated in the verse spoken by the Venerable Kumāralāta:
"All realms of existence are transformations, Except for the Śuddhāvāsa heavens;
Transforming in various ways according to karma, There is no place where they do not take birth."

For this reason, it is known that all bodhisattvas always share the same purpose of benefiting others; they guide and transform beings according to where they take birth. By the power of skillful means, they act solely for the sake of sentient beings, and are not bound by the retribution of afflictions or karma.
As the Venerable Deva said in verse:
"Sometimes appearing as a teacher, And sometimes acting as a disciple,
By means of various skillful methods, He transforms all the ignorant and foolish."
"Exercising mastery over all realms of existence, one is always honored by the multitude;
yet if there are those who do not show such honor, this is the karma of great arrogance.
Therefore, although a bodhisattva may wear the robes and appearance of a layperson, they ought to receive salutations and respect.
It is just as the Tathāgata, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, manifests various forms.

For example, he manifested as an old bhikṣu to transform King Pukkasāti; he manifested as a potter, as a wrestler, and as a master of lutes, harps, and arts; and he likewise appeared in various forms of householders.
Although they may assume various and immeasurable forms, all should be revered and prostrated to.
Therefore, even if they wear the same attire as worldly people, one should pay them increased respect and honor.
As the Buddha said in a verse:
“Adorning all practices with tranquility, Taming oneself, being resolute, and cultivating the holy life,
Relinquishing the sword and staff toward all sentient beings— These are called śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.”
Therefore, one should not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding Bodhisattvas by grasping at their physical forms or appearances.

Bodhisattvas serve as a great dwelling for all sentient beings within the three realms; they may manifest as Buddhas, or as devas and humans, or even manifest as various kinds of animals. In all such cases, one should pay homage to the Bodhisattva’s wondrous accumulation of merit;
one should not form a mind that pays homage to their outward appearance, as worldly people do when paying respects to mere images.
If one reveres the Dharma-body from afar, how could such reverence reside in metal, stone, clay, wood, or earth?
Therefore, when Bodhisattvas employ various skillful means to manifest internal and external forms to benefit sentient beings, there is no fault in paying them homage.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is neither in nirvāṇa nor not in nirvāṇa, as expressed in the verse spoken by Rāhula:
“Suffering in birth and death is long and far-reaching; One ought to enter nirvāṇa.
Yet by the power of great compassion, He dwells for a long time and does not abandon us.”

Therefore, you should know that throughout the long duration of birth and death, the Dharma-body is eternally abiding while the form-body manifests in response; it is like the extinguishing of a lamp. For this reason, the Dharma-body of a Bodhisattva is superior to the form-bodies of all Buddhas.

The form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the dharma-bodies (*dharmakāya*) of the Bodhisattvas abide in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

The dharma-bodies of the Bodhisattvas abide in the all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the Buddhas; as for the form-bodies of the Buddhas, they manifest for the sake of transforming sentient beings, causing Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others to pay them all reverence.

Therefore, the Buddha taught that making offerings to the physical bodies of sixty-two billion Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is not equal to making an offering to a single Dharma-body of a Bodhisattva.
As stated in the *Sarvapuṇyasamuccayasamādhi-sūtra*, one should take joy and delight in the True Dharma.
One must never say that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, as the verse in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"Always dwelling on Vulture Peak, And at all other places of residence;..."
"Ordinary, foolish, and ignorant ones do not see it, even though they are present.
As stated in the *Sarvalokadhātupraveśamahāvyūhasamādhisūtra*, it says to a son of good family:
"Do you see the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Indeed, I have seen it."
Within a single pore, one sees billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds; his physical and verbal karma pervades all these Buddha-worlds.

Furthermore, as stated in the *Tathāgataguhyaka*, when the Bodhisattva Kṣiprābha held the contemplation of the Tathāgata’s crown, he could not see it even by ascending to immeasurable Buddha-worlds above.
For example, when Maudgalyāyana sought to follow the sounds of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-teaching, he could not reach the end of the Buddha’s voice even as far as the world-system of Gaganagañja.

As described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, while the Tathāgata remains within his palace, he manifests throughout immeasurable worlds his initial birth, his turning of the wheel of Dharma, and his entry into nirvāṇa.

As stated in the *Guhyagarbha Sūtra*, the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata dwells within the bodies of all sentient beings, manifesting externally like a reflection; it is just as a mani jewel wrapped in pure silk, which remains entirely unobstructed.
Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body pervades all sentient beings.
As the Buddha has taught, even withered trees and scorched wood are entirely included within it and should not be harmed, let alone other types of beings.
Therefore, one should not attempt to measure sentient beings, for none except the Tathāgatas are able to know them.
As Vimalakīrti has said, all Buddha-fields are entirely adorned and pure; this Sahā world is likewise so.

Because sentient beings of great resolve possess the Tathāgatagarbha, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, through skillful means, causes the great disciples among the śrāvakas to manifest in this world of five turbidities.

Although various non-Buddhists calculate [the self] in terms of identity or difference, such persons likewise possess the Dharma-body within their entire bodies; all are born from the skillful means of Bodhisattvas and are intended to manifest the Mahāyāna path.

Therefore, you should know that because Bodhisattvas teach and transform sentient beings within the trichiliocosm, their methods are diverse and not uniform. For those with sharp faculties, they praise the Mahāyāna so that there is no cause for disparagement or suspicion, and their minds may easily understand it.

For those with dull faculties who have entered the forest of false views and are ensnared by the net of ignorance, they enable them to encounter Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; through these causes and conditions, they extinguish all false views and thereby enter the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna is the most fundamental among all vehicles.

If there are sentient beings who receive, uphold, believe in, and understand this Mahāyāna, you should know that their karmic retributions and afflictions will all be eliminated. This is as stated in the *Sūtra on the Lord’s Dispelling All Doubts and Remorse for King Ajātaśatru*: "O Prabhāsa!"
Do not speak such words.

Why is this? If you were to practice various meditative concentrations for ten kalpas in other Buddha-worlds, it would not equal practicing the mind of loving-kindness for even a single meal’s duration in this Sahā world.
Why is this? Even if one were to sever the afflictions in other worlds, it would not equal the cultivation of wholesome karma within a single meal’s duration in this Sahā world.
As stated in the *Prophecy for Mañjuśrī* and as fully detailed in other sūtras:

if there are sentient beings who slander the true Dharma, the transgressions and heinous crimes of such slandering the Dharma are extensively explained in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
However, if one can receive, uphold, believe, and understand the Mahāyāna, even the five ānantarya sins will all be completely extinguished.
As the Buddha said in a verse:
"Those who have committed grave and evil deeds, If they can deeply repent and reproach themselves,
And reverently believe in the Mahāyāna Dharma, They shall uproot all roots of sin."

When the Buddha taught such true characteristics of phenomena, the successive continuity of faithful mind flowed on in an unbroken stream, entirely empty and quiescent; thus, all previously committed evils were immediately extinguished.
As the Blessed One said in the *Vimatividhamana-sūtra*:
"Great King!
Examine your own mind: with what state of mind did you kill your father?"
Is it the past mind, the future mind, or the present mind?
If it is the past mind, the past mind has already ceased; if the mind has already ceased, it has no location and no place of abiding.
If it is a future mind, the future mind has not yet arrived.
If it is a present mind, the present mind does not abide.

It is like a magical illusion: it is neither blue, yellow, red, white, purple, nor crystal-colored; its essential nature is purely pristine, even to the point of being neither a characteristic nor visible.
When explained in detail in this manner, one immediately attains the superior realms.
Therefore, it should be known that the Mahāyāna is the fundamental vehicle.

As stated in the *Maitreya-vyūha-sūtra* regarding the practice of generating the bodhicitta: by understanding the bodhicitta and abiding in the bodhicitta, one obtains great benefit and does not fall into the evil realms.

Understanding the bodhicitta and purifying the bodhicitta, one gradually increases [these qualities] from stage to stage until attaining the dharmakāya, and is able to manifest supernatural powers as the transformations performed by Vairocana Buddha.
And he spoke in verse:
“If one attains a stainless body, Its form and appearance are then immeasurable;
Sometimes appearing in Jambudvīpa, Or dwelling in Tuṣita.”
From the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha until the very end of birth and death,
knowing the opportune and the inopportune— this should be known as the transformation of Dīpaṃkara.
It is not a place of form or color, nor is it the signless.
All arise from fundamental practice, like the moon reflected in water.
Body, speech, and mind are all secret; these are all the unshared dharmas.
Throughout all worlds, the form-body manifests liberation.
All the devas and humans of the world who wish to behold the Buddha’s crown—
boundless and inconceivable, surpassing billions of worlds—
even Maudgalyāyana and his disciples seek the Buddha’s voice with a sincere heart.
Transcending even hundreds of thousands of worlds, its sound reaches out boundlessly.
The merits and deeds of the Dharma-body cannot be known by anyone;
they cannot be fully proclaimed through forms or the artistry of words.
Seeing and hearing this is solely through the power of the Buddha; it is not within my own realm.
Those who wish to repay the Buddha’s kindness should receive this with their heads bowed, believe it, and practice accordingly.
Now, the Dharma I have preached, I dedicate in turn to all sentient beings.
Having completely extinguished the fetters of affliction, one attains realization of the unsurpassed path.
*Introduction to the Mahāyāna*, Scroll Lower.
